articles.headline: Update: Washington extends its chip controls to data centres worldwide, and Beijing calls it “economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction”
articles.summary:
**On 16 November the US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule on remote access to advanced “super intelligence” (SI) chips and servers.**

BIS says the rule was “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council” and that it is meant to stop existing restrictions from being circumvented “through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries”. The rule adds a new end-use control: a licence is required to ship advanced chips and servers to a data centre **anywhere in the world** that provides more than 12 million “aggregate TPP” of compute to companies headquartered (or whose ultimate parent is headquartered) in China, another Country Group D:5 destination or Macau. That means European data centres are covered too, if they serve such customers. Data centres already serving those customers must obtain a licence within 90 days or “face future export restrictions”, and exports of advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil now need a licence because of a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to China. The same day, White House science and technology director Michael Kratsios announced the carrot that goes with the stick: Commerce designated 33 preset consortia under the “American SI Exports Program”, full-stack US AI packages backed by priority licensing, advocacy and financing from Commerce, State, EXIM, DFC, USTDA, Treasury, USTR and SBA, so that “U.S. technology [is] the easiest, most attractive choice for allies and partners”. @F_CEAFE reposted the House China Select Committee’s announcement, Kratsios’s post, the Commerce–Justice statement on the Megaspeed probe, an analyst’s thread on the rule and, at 11:09 Madrid, the Chinese Foreign Ministry’s response.

**China’s reaction (linked):** At the MFA’s regular press conference on 17 November, spokesperson Guo Jiakun said: “The move is yet another case of the U.S. overstretching the concept of national security, and abusing export control measures to interfere in normal trade and tech cooperation between China and other countries and go after China’s high-tech industry. Such typical economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction run counter to the common understandings between the two countries, harm the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies, and disrupt global supply chains. China will do what is necessary to firmly safeguard its legitimate and lawful rights and interests.” Asked about Megaspeed, he said China’s position on US chip exports to China “is consistent”. On MOFCOM’s Spokesman’s Remarks page, the latest item at about 11:45 Madrid was still the 13 November statement on the Unreliable Entity List, so the ministry had not issued a separate statement yet. Global Times (Chinese state media) and CGTN (Chinese state media) carried the MFA line, and CGTN framed it as China accusing the US of “economic coercion and overreach”.
articles.why: This is an extraterritorial rule in the full sense. A US agency, acting on Treasury and NSC instructions, now decides which customers a data centre in Frankfurt, Dublin or Madrid may serve if it runs American chips. The rule removes the de minimis exemption for this end use and expects data centres to hand their “know your customer” checks to exporters, where a refusal counts as a red flag. Europe has no chip of its own in this class: the continent’s fastest supercomputer, JUPITER, runs on NVIDIA GH200. EU cloud and AI providers therefore follow Washington’s China policy whether or not the EU has agreed to it, just as Europeans already did on Iranian and Venezuelan oil, Huawei in 5G networks and the frozen EU–China investment agreement (CAI). The “American SI Exports Program” finishes the picture: allies are offered subsidised US stacks on condition of “trusted” use. Beijing’s warning of “necessary measures” could land on European firms caught in the middle, as the Nexperia case showed. Here is another example of why Europeans need to act together: only a common European compute and chip base would let Europe decide its own export rules.
articles.watch: Federal Register publication (19 Nov) and the start of the 90-day clock; whether MOFCOM announces countermeasures (Unreliable Entity List, rare-earth or other export controls); whether the Commission or the Dutch, Irish and German governments say anything on the rule’s reach into EU data centres; the Trump–Xi meeting in Shenzhen (19 Nov) and the US–China truce that runs to 10 January. Earlier coverage: 16 Nov 07:30–20:30 and 17 Nov 07:30.

articles.headline: Megaspeed: Washington details a chip-smuggling dragnet that runs through Singapore
articles.summary:
**The US Commerce and Justice departments released a joint statement on their investigation of Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud-computing company and Nvidia customer.**

According to the statement as reported by CNBC and SCMP, Commerce began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 for possible export-control violations and asked Nvidia for its sales records in May 2025; Nvidia put Megaspeed on its “no sell” list in June 2025, and the Justice Department then took over the criminal investigation. The statement also says 17 defendants in six separate investigations have been charged with smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of semiconductors. Vice President JD Vance said the administration was concerned about any reports that a third country had obtained Nvidia technology (Reuters post). Singapore is now seeking talks with Washington on the AI chip rules (SCMP). Separately, Reuters reported in an exclusive that Chinese entities are using increasingly sophisticated ways to use output from leading American AI models to train domestic rivals as chip curbs bite.
articles.why: The probe is the enforcement arm of the rule in topic 1. Third-country hubs like Singapore now carry the burden of proving their customers are clean, which is exactly what European data centres will be asked to do. A European AI industry that depends on US chips also inherits US investigations, “no sell” lists and the legal risk Nvidia is now passing on to its buyers (CNBC via Reuters post).
articles.watch: charges or Entity List designations tied to Megaspeed; Singapore–US talks; Nvidia’s results and its new export-control board committee.

articles.headline: China’s envoy in Madrid: Europe should “not follow the instructions of others” on ASML chip-tool exports
articles.summary:
**In an interview with Reuters in Madrid, Qu Xun, China’s minister-counsellor in Spain, said long-standing Dutch limits on exporting ASML chipmaking equipment to China are casting a shadow over EU–China industrial-policy talks.**

“We want the European Union to make its own decisions and not follow the instructions of others,” he said, adding: “We want to import ASML goods.” He warned that “Europe is forbidding it because it is afraid China will rob its technology… If Europe thinks that way, China will too”, implying that China could limit the sharing of its own technology. Reuters notes that the Netherlands has restricted ASML exports to China since 2019 and that the US is pushing for curbs on lower-level machines, with stricter controls under discussion in Congress that would also hit Japan’s Tokyo Electron. Qu said China seeks “equality and reciprocity” as the EU weighs local-content, technology-transfer and ownership conditions on foreign investors in EVs, batteries and cars. He also said Chinese investment in Spain has tripled in a decade to €12 billion, with SAIC, Chery, CATL and AESC among the investors.
articles.why: This is the other side of topic 1. ASML is Europe’s one undisputed world chokepoint in semiconductors, and its exports to China are set by Dutch licences shaped by US pressure. Beijing is now openly linking that alignment to Europe’s access to Chinese battery and EV technology, which is exactly what Spain is trying to attract. CEAFE’s point is that Europe should decide its export policy as a bloc, on its own interests, rather than member by member under pressure from either Washington or Beijing.
articles.watch: any Dutch or Commission reply; US congressional moves on chip-tool controls; MOFCOM’s line on EU investment conditions.

articles.headline: TOP500: China keeps the world’s fastest supercomputer on a fully Chinese stack, while Europe’s best runs on American chips
articles.why: Measured together, the EU-27 is a real second pole in supercomputing; measured country by country, no member state comes close to the US or China. Europe’s flagship machine depends on US processors, the very kind of hardware whose use Washington now regulates worldwide, whereas China has built its No. 1 on its own chips, interconnect and operating system. The European Processor Initiative and EuroHPC exist precisely to close that gap. The EU as a whole can bear comparison; each capital on its own cannot. That is the difference that matters.
articles.watch: next list June 2027; EuroHPC’s next exascale system (Alice Recoque, France). Rankings file updated.

articles.headline: China’s Sinochem cuts its Pirelli stake to 13.6% after Italy’s “golden power” curbs
articles.summary:
**Marco Polo International Italy, the vehicle of Chinese state-owned Sinochem (CNRC), sold 70 million Pirelli shares (6.5% of the capital) in an accelerated bookbuild run by BNP Paribas at €6.50 per share, about €455 million, a 3.8% discount to Monday’s close.**

Its stake falls from 20.1% to about 13.6%, behind Marco Tronchetti Provera’s Camfin/MTP (29.9%) and Czech billionaire Michal Strnad (about 14%), who bought 14% from Sinochem earlier this year at the same price. Pirelli shares fell more than 3% in Milan. The retreat follows Rome’s use of its “golden power” screening: an April decree limited Sinochem to three of the 15 board seats, with no executive roles or strategic powers, and those restrictions apply while its stake exceeds 9.99%. Italian press links the intervention to protecting Pirelli’s Cyber Tyre technology and the company’s access to the US tyre market. A 90-day lock-up applies to the remaining stake (Websim/Intermonte).
articles.why: This is the European version of the “blocking Chinese control” track the owner asked us to follow: a member state used FDI screening to push a Chinese state shareholder out of a strategic industrial company, partly so as not to lose access to the US market. Italian screening worked, but it was a national decision; the EU still has no common instrument to decide such cases, and alignment with US connected-vehicle rules is shaping European ownership choices. Note: @F_CEAFE has not posted this story.
articles.watch: whether Sinochem drops below 10% after the lock-up, lifting the golden-power conditions; any MOFCOM or Sinochem comment.

articles.headline: Commission autumn forecast: growth holds at 1.2% in the euro area, but the energy shock keeps inflation above 3%
articles.summary:
**The European Commission’s Autumn 2026 Economic Forecast (17 November) expects EU GDP growth of 1.4% in 2026 and 2027 and 1.5% in 2028, and 1.2%, 1.2% and 1.3% in the euro area.**

Inflation is forecast at 3.3% (EU) and 3.2% (euro area) in 2026, easing to 2.3% and 2.1% only in 2028. The Commission blames the Middle East war: energy flows through Hormuz “remain severely disrupted”, Brent exceeded $100 in October, diesel prices doubled year on year and TTF gas traded above €95/MWh in late October, more than three times its late-February level, with thin buffers in strategic reserves and gas storage. Central banks, including the Fed, have started or are expected to raise rates, and the 10-year US Treasury yield was about 5.1% at the cut-off. Deficits widen to −3.6% of GDP in the EU in 2026 and −3.8% in 2028. Bloomberg summarised it as robust growth despite stubborn inflation.
articles.why: The forecast puts a number on Europe’s energy dependence: imported fossil fuels are again the main driver of inflation and of the rate rises that tighten financing for defence and industrial investment. The Commission itself lists faster progress in the energy transition “to reduce Europe’s dependence on imported fossil fuels” and stronger investment in defence and industry as upside factors.
articles.watch: Eurostat’s final October HICP; the ECB’s December meeting.

Update: The chip rule hits Asian markets as Trump’s aides fight over China
Macron in Kuala Lumpur: rare earths and defence, as Malaysia questions Western suppliers

articles.headline: Brussels sets a precedent: EU anti-dumping duties now count the knock-on effect of Chinese overcapacity
articles.summary:
**The European Commission imposed definitive anti-dumping duties on 16 November on cold-rolled flat steel from India, Japan, Taiwan, Türkiye and Vietnam.**

For the first time in an EU trade-defence case it established “Particular Market Situations”, which let it construct the normal value instead of using distorted domestic prices. In India the distortion came from government measures on the price of iron ore. In Taiwan, the Commission found that Chinese overcapacity had pushed Chinese cold-rolled steel into the Taiwanese market, depressing local prices and the profitability of Taiwanese producers. In other words, Brussels now treats the price-depressing effect of Chinese overcapacity on third countries as something it can correct for (the “push-out” effect, in the words of the law firm Gide, which worked on the case). The Commission calls the investigation “of systemic importance for trade defence, beyond the products and industry sectors it concerns”, and Bloomberg reports that it is preparing further tools and assessing safeguards for chemicals and machinery.

**China’s reaction (linked):** No MOFCOM statement on this case was found by 05:45 Madrid. MOFCOM has already criticised France and Germany’s request for stronger EU trade-defence tools (10 October) and reports of a European “Section 301”-style instrument (30 September). Watch MOFCOM’s next briefing.
articles.why: This is the EU using its own legal toolbox to protect a strategic industry (12 producing member states, more than 8,600 jobs), rather than copying Washington’s tariffs. The duties hit partners, not China directly, so the real test is whether Brussels uses the same reasoning against the source of the overcapacity, and against anyone else, including the US, whose subsidies distort markets. A Union of 27 can set precedents like this. No member state alone could.
articles.watch: MOFCOM reaction; whether the new trade-defence tools and the chemicals and machinery safeguards are announced; whether partners such as India or Japan challenge the duties at the WTO.

articles.headline: Update: The chip rule hits Asian markets as Trump’s aides fight over China
articles.summary:
**New facts since the 20:30 edition: Monday’s sell-off in Taiwan was the second-largest one-day point loss in the TAIEX’s history, at −6.03% to 41,040.**

TSMC fell 5.74%, Foxconn 9.34% and MediaTek 7.89%, with 17 high-priced stocks limit-down (Taiwan News). Barclays blamed forced retail liquidation. On Tuesday morning, after the BIS rule, the Nikkei was down 0.9% (Advantest −3.9%, SoftBank −3.8%), the Kospi was down 1.0% (Samsung −2.0%, SK hynix −1.1%) and Singapore was down 0.6% (Dow Jones/MarketScreener). UOB estimates that the move erased about $960 bn in US tech market value. Bloomberg reports that Chinese model developer Z.ai has fallen 85% from its peak as chip fears hit Chinese AI firms. In Washington, the Washington Post and WSJ describe an open feud between Treasury Secretary Bessent and Commerce Secretary Lutnick over Nvidia chips. Hours after the crackdown, Trump said he understood “both sides”.

**China’s reaction (linked):** Still no MOFCOM statement on the final rule by 05:45 Madrid. The latest official line found is the Foreign Ministry’s of 13 November: China “opposes abuse of export control measures” and urges both sides to deliver on the “common understandings between the two presidents”. Watch the Shenzhen summit.
articles.why: Washington’s chip policy now moves markets across Asia and is being made through a personal fight inside the cabinet. That is a fragile base for European clouds and for ASML, which must comply with it. Europe still has no equivalent lever of its own.
articles.watch: Trump–Xi summit in Shenzhen; MOFCOM; European chip stocks (ASML, Infineon, STMicro) at today’s open.

articles.headline: Macron in Kuala Lumpur: rare earths and defence, as Malaysia questions Western suppliers
articles.summary:
**President Emmanuel Macron is meeting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim on 17 November, on his first visit to Malaysia since 2017, to upgrade relations to a “strategic partnership” and sign several MoUs on defence, trade, the energy transition and critical minerals.**

Macron said that a key aim is to diversify France’s sources of rare earths: “having several sources of supply means reducing the risk of having to halt production lines”. The French firm Carester and the Malaysian miner Malaco are working on a mining and processing project that includes a separation plant in Perak with an estimated capacity of about 13,000 tonnes of rare earths a year. France is also offering help on Malaysia’s move from chip packaging into chip design. Malaysia is reassessing foreign arms suppliers after Norway revoked an export licence for missiles for its navy. Its defence minister said this raised questions about the trustworthiness of Western and NATO partners (France 24/Reuters).
articles.why: It is a concrete European move to break China’s grip on rare earths without relying on US-led clubs. But it is still one member state acting alone, and it competes with Germany’s and others’ efforts. The Norway episode shows how export-licence politics can close markets to European industry. Pooled EU purchasing and stockpiling of critical raw materials, and predictable European export rules, would carry more weight than national deals.
articles.watch: Texts of the MoUs signed today; any defence contract; EU Critical Raw Materials Act projects.

articles.headline: Update: Oil drops below $93 despite more tanker attacks; Houthis close in on Bab el-Mandeb
articles.summary:
**New facts since the 20:30 edition: Brent settled down 3.6% at $92.44 a barrel on Monday and WTI 3.2% lower at $85.72.**

In Asian trading on Tuesday Brent was around $92. Recovering Middle East exports point to a surplus: the IEA expects the market to return to surplus in Q4, and Saudi Arabia pumped 10.5 mb/d in October (ANZ). The risks have not gone away, though. The IRGC claims that two more tankers hit mines (not independently verified), UKMTO reported two tanker attacks off Khasab, Oman, and the IMO has recorded 136 security incidents involving vessels in the region since 1 March, 35 of them in October. In Yemen, Houthi fighters have advanced to about 100 km from Aden after government forces left positions near the Bab el-Mandeb, the strait used by Saudi crude shipped from Yanbu, which has been the kingdom’s main export outlet since the Iran war began. Iran warns of severe gas shortages this winter (Al Jazeera, Reuters).
articles.why: Cheaper oil hides a fragile supply: both chokepoints feeding Europe and Asia are contested at once. Europe has no naval or energy-security instrument of its own at that scale, and it depends on Saudi rerouting and on US decisions. The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at its lowest since 1982 after a 172 m-barrel release, so Washington’s buffer is thinner too.
articles.watch: TTF and EU storage today; OPEC+ on 29 November; Houthi moves around Aden.

articles.headline: A US Pentagon loan props up Wolfspeed, Infineon’s silicon carbide wafer supplier
articles.summary:
**Wolfspeed (Durham, North Carolina), the silicon carbide (SiC) materials and power-chip maker, reported revenue of $155 m for the quarter to 27 September.**

That is down 21% year on year but up 3.6% on the previous quarter. Its net loss was $111.4 m. AI data centres were its fastest-growing market. The company is building its recovery on a conditional 30-year, $1.5 bn loan commitment from the US Department of War “to advance the domestic supply chain for wide-bandgap semiconductors”. The first $600 m tranche refinances costly debt, and later tranches would fund domestic GaN power devices, GaN-on-SiC RF materials and radiation-hardening capabilities. During the quarter Wolfspeed extended its long-term SiC wafer supply agreement with Germany’s Infineon from 150 mm to 200 mm wafers (Semiconductor Today).
articles.why: Washington treats SiC and GaN, which are key to electric vehicles, radar and electronic warfare, as national security and funds its champion through the defence budget. Europe’s largest power-semiconductor maker, Infineon, deepens its reliance on that US-backed supplier. Europe has SiC capacity of its own (STMicro in Catania, Soitec), and the EU Chips Act and EDF should treat this as a sovereignty issue in the same way.
articles.watch: Final terms of the US government loan; Infineon’s SiC sourcing strategy.

articles.headline: Update: Washington closes the “remote access” loophole and extends chip controls to data centres worldwide
articles.summary:
**The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule on 16 November, “written by and at the direction of” the Treasury and the National Security Council, to stop companies headquartered in China and other Country Group D:5 destinations (or Macau) from using advanced US AI chips remotely through data centres in third countries.**

Any data centre anywhere in the world that supplies more than 12 million “aggregate TPP” of compute to such companies now needs a licence, and chip exporters, foundries and data-centre operators must check their customers’ direct and indirect ownership. The rule also adds a licence requirement for advanced chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, except when the buyer is a US-headquartered company, and formally rescinds the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. It comes three days before the Trump–Xi meeting in Shenzhen and after the Nvidia espionage scandal; a US senator has accused Commerce of failing to stem chip flows to China, while President Trump expressed confidence in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick (Reuters, Bloomberg). Previous coverage: 07:30 and 13:30 editions, topic 1.

**China’s reaction (linked):** No MOFCOM statement on the new rule was found by 18:45 Madrid. On 13 November, when the measure was still a bill, China’s Foreign Ministry opposed the “abuse” of export controls. Reuters quotes analysts saying that the scandal “is going to embolden China hawks and rock this very fragile trade truce”. Beijing’s counter-levers are covered in topic 5. Watch MOFCOM and the summit.

**ALERT — not yet reposted by @F_CEAFE:** US export-control story with extraterritorial reach to European data centres. No @F_CEAFE post on it in the window. Link: https://media.bis.gov/press-release/bis-issues-rule-addressing-remote-access-american-super-intelligence-technology
articles.why: The rule is extraterritorial. It applies to data centres “to or within any destination worldwide”, including European clouds, which must now vet their customers’ ownership for Washington. It also writes a US-only exemption into law: in the five “diversion-risk” countries, chips for US-headquartered companies need no licence, but chips for European ones do. This is the US double standard in regulatory form, with American industrial leadership treated as national security and enforced on allies’ soil. Europe has no comparable instrument to protect its own technology and complies through ASML and its cloud operators without reciprocity.
articles.watch: Federal Register publication and comment period; MOFCOM response; Trump–Xi Shenzhen summit (19 Nov); whether the Commission or EU cloud providers comment on the due-diligence burden.

articles.headline: Brussels clears UniCredit–Commerzbank, the largest cross-border bank deal since the financial crisis
articles.summary:
**The European Commission gave unconditional approval on 16 November under the EU Merger Regulation to UniCredit’s acquisition of control of Commerzbank, Germany’s second-largest bank.**

The US Federal Reserve also approved it the same day, and UniCredit expects the last outstanding approval by the end of November. Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera called it “probably the biggest cross-border banking deal we have had since the financial crisis” and a model of “positive scaling up of EU banks”. Unusually, she warned that Brussels would “react accordingly” if a national government tried to block completion (Politico). Berlin, which still holds about 13% of Commerzbank, is demanding guarantees on jobs, the Frankfurt headquarters and two supervisory-board seats.
articles.why: This is a European champion built inside the single market, not a sale to an outside buyer. Even combined, UniCredit and Commerzbank would be worth only about a fifth of JPMorgan (Politico). That gap is the scale argument for the banking union and for capital-markets integration that can finance European defence and industry. It also tests whether member states will put national control ahead of building European scale.
articles.watch: Berlin’s response; the final approval by end-November; the merger-guidelines reform.

articles.headline: Energy: oil slides to about $95 despite Hormuz mine attacks, but Europe’s gas cushion stays thin
articles.summary:
**Brent fell 0.7% to $95.15 a barrel and WTI to $88.19 on Monday (Reuters via CNBC), extending a two-week slide.**

The IEA said on Friday that the oil market will return to surplus in Q4, with supply at 105 mb/d, 1.7 mb/d above demand, as Middle East exports recover. This happened even though Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said two more tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, after six caught fire on Sunday and Monday (claims not independently verified). Dutch TTF gas slipped below €90/MWh on milder weather, the expected end of Norway’s Troll outage and record pipeline flows to US LNG plants (21.8 bcf on Saturday, BloombergNEF). EU storage, however, was 70.5% full on 14 November, 19.5 points below the five-year norm, and QatarEnergy has extended its force majeure until at least the end of December. Previous coverage: 13:30 edition, topic 3.
articles.why: Lower prices come from US LNG and an IEA stock release, not from European resilience. Europe is swapping dependence on Gulf and Russian gas for dependence on US cargoes, which are exactly what Washington asks it to buy. The low storage level leaves the winter exposed to any new shock.
articles.watch: EU storage trajectory against the 1 December target; Qatar force majeure; Hormuz shipping data.

articles.headline: China’s export-control lever: rare-earth champions double profits, tunnel-boring machine curbs start Wednesday
articles.summary:
**China’s two rare-earth national champions more than doubled their nine-month profits.**

China Northern Rare Earth earned 3.65 bn yuan ($547 m) and China Rare Earth Resources and Technology 408 m yuan, as production quotas and consolidation pushed prices up (Reuters via Mining Weekly). NdPr oxide, the main magnet input, trades at 719,000 yuan a tonne, 62% above its level when the April 2025 export controls were introduced. Common magnets are not controlled, and China exported 48,057 t of them in January–September, up from 39,826 t a year earlier. Separately, Beijing’s new export controls on tunnel-boring machines take effect on 18 November. Exports to “sensitive” countries with territorial disputes, including India, will need a MOFCOM licence, which could delay metro, high-speed-rail and Himalayan-border tunnelling projects (The Hindu, Times of India). Bloomberg notes that US dependence on Chinese supplies “goes far beyond” rare earths.
articles.why: This is the counterpart to topic 1. China answers US controls with its own, and the profits show that the lever pays. Europe faces the same dependence on Chinese rare earths but neither builds an equivalent lever nor answers either side. The Critical Raw Materials Act targets are the test.
articles.watch: Whether Beijing uses rare earths against the BIS rule after the summit; how India responds to the tunnel-boring machine licences.

articles.headline: Reverse flow: Italy’s Maire buys US LNG liquefaction technology from Baker Hughes
articles.summary:
**Maire’s Nextchem unit agreed to buy Chart Industries’ mid-scale IPSMR and small-scale LNG process technologies, with more than 90 patents, for $220 million in cash.**

Chart is a wholly owned subsidiary of Baker Hughes. The deal includes a 10-year cold-box supply agreement and a 12-person team, and is expected to close by the end of 2026 or in early January 2027, subject to regulatory approvals (Maire press release, 15 Nov). Maire shares rose 3.6% on Monday (Reuters).
articles.why: This time a European firm acquires US intellectual property and know-how in a strategic energy technology, the opposite of the usual flow of European technology into US hands. It gives Europe a licensing position in LNG liquefaction at a time when European energy security depends on LNG. Watch whether US authorities impose conditions.
articles.watch: Regulatory approvals before closing.

articles.headline: A €1 bn fund for European deep tech: Plural, an early Helsing backer, closes Fund 3
articles.summary:
**UK-based Plural raised €1 billion ($1.1 bn) for its third fund to back European start-ups in energy, AI infrastructure, defence and healthcare.**

Two-thirds will go to early-stage deals and one-third to follow-ons (Reuters via StreetInsider, TechCrunch). In a post reposted on the R&D list on 16 November, Commissioner Ekaterina Zaharieva highlighted the €5 billion Scaleup Europe Fund at the European Startup and Scaleup Forum.
articles.why: Private European capital going into defence and AI start-ups reduces the need to sell growing companies to US buyers. Fund sizes still lag US venture capital, and the Scaleup Europe Fund is meant to close that late-stage gap.
articles.watch: First investments; Scaleup Europe Fund deployment.

Europe in the red, China past $1 trillion: the trade gap in numbers

articles.headline: Update: Washington crowns its AI “national champions” as chip curbs loom over the Trump–Xi summit
articles.summary:
**The Wall Street Journal reported on 15 November that the Trump administration plans to designate more than two dozen AI “national champions”, including Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic, to help them win business abroad against Chinese rivals; Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick could unveil the list within a week (WSJ via Reuters, The Next Web).**

Designated packages may get government advocacy, federal financing and faster export-licence reviews under the American AI Exports Program created by a July 2025 executive order. At the same time, Reuters reports that the prospect of tighter US curbs on China’s access to advanced AI chips, pushed by lawmakers after Jensen Huang’s resignation, is likely to overshadow the Trump–Xi meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday 19 November; a US official said there will be no further progress on the “Board of Trade” plan to cut reciprocal tariffs on $30 billion of goods. Previous coverage: 07:30 edition, topic 1.

**China’s reaction (linked):** Chinese analysts quoted by the South China Morning Post (13 Nov) say Beijing could tighten rare-earth export controls if Washington escalates chip curbs; Victor Gao (Centre for China and Globalisation) called using the Nvidia affair to pressure Beijing a “complete miscalculation”. China’s expanded rare-earth controls remain suspended until 10 January 2027. No official MOFCOM statement yet; Global Times (Chinese state media) reported Bessent’s demands on Nvidia without comment. Watch the summit.

**ALERT — not yet reposted by @F_CEAFE:** US industrial-policy / export-control story (national champions + chip curbs, China rare-earth counter-lever). @F_CEAFE has reposted the summit announcements (Mao Ning, Global Times) but not this angle. Link: https://thenextweb.com/news/ai-national-champions-nvidia-openai-anthropic-trump
articles.why: This is the US double standard in one week: Washington names state-backed national champions, finances their exports and controls who buys their chips, while asking Europe not to be protectionist and to buy American. Europe has no equivalent list, no joint export-finance package for its own AI and cloud firms, and follows US chip controls (ASML) without reciprocity. A Buy-European logic for AI infrastructure would be the mirror image.
articles.watch: Commerce announcement of the list; Nvidia Q3 results (18 Nov); Shenzhen summit (19 Nov) and any MOFCOM measure; NDAA chip amendments.

articles.headline: Europe in the red, China past $1 trillion: the trade gap in numbers
articles.summary:
**Eurostat published on 16 November that euro-area industrial production rose 0.2% m/m in September (EU +0.5%) but is down 1.5% y/y (EU −0.8%).**

Its 13 November releases show euro-area Q3 GDP up 0.4% q/q (+1.3% y/y; EU +0.5% and +1.5%), against +0.8% q/q in the United States, and a euro-area goods trade deficit of €10.3 billion in September, against a €13.5 billion surplus a year earlier, driven by a wider energy deficit (€33.0 bn vs €20.7 bn) and a shrinking machinery-and-vehicles surplus (€3.0 bn vs €10.0 bn). Over January–September the euro area ran a €36.5 bn deficit, compared with a €102.2 bn surplus a year earlier. China, by contrast, posted a $1.04 trillion surplus in January–October, the fastest it has ever reached that mark, with October exports +35.2% y/y on AI hardware, while domestic demand keeps disappointing (WSJ, CNBC, AP). Ahead of APEC, Premier Li Qiang hailed China–ASEAN achievements “in the face of global trade restrictions”, and ASEAN signed its Digital Economy Framework Agreement in Manila (Xinhua, Chinese state media).
articles.why: Europe now imports more than it exports, because it pays for energy it does not produce and its industrial surplus is eroding, while China’s surplus keeps growing. No single Member State can answer this alone. Only the EU, acting as one trade power, can set common trade defence and a European preference.
articles.watch: Eurostat final HICP for October; Commission autumn forecast; EU trade-defence cases against Chinese overcapacity.

articles.headline: Update: Gas stays near €90 as Europe enters winter with the lowest storage since 2013
articles.summary:
**Dutch TTF front-month gas eased 0.5% to €90.50/MWh on Monday morning and UK NBP to 225.90 p/therm, while Brent for January fell 0.9% to $95.00/bbl, extending a two-week slide (Investing.com, 16 Nov).**

Bloomberg says traders weighed milder weather and record US exports against Europe’s thin winter inventories. The IEA’s Global Gas Security Review 2026 (3 Nov) says EU storage entered the heating season at its lowest since 2013, after the effective halt of LNG through Hormuz cut Qatari and Emirati loadings by more than 60 bcm between March and October; tight markets could last well into 2027. The IEA also says 71 million barrels of emergency stocks will be released by the end of February. Copper fell for a third day to a four-month low on the tech selloff and weak Chinese data (Bloomberg). Previous coverage: 07:30 edition, topic 2.
articles.why: Europe is replacing one dependence (Russian pipeline gas) with another (US LNG) at prices far above pre-crisis levels. The energy deficit is the main reason the euro area is now in trade deficit (topic 2). Common purchasing, storage obligations and faster European generation are a matter of sovereignty.
articles.watch: EU storage withdrawals (AGSI); US EIA STEO; Brent reaction to the Bahrain strike reports (military side: see Conflicts).

articles.headline: Paying for Ukraine and squeezing Russia: €45 bn EU-budget loan and a Finnish push on “war crypto”
articles.summary:
**The Financial Times reported on 16 November that the Commission will propose on Wednesday a new loan of about €45 billion, borrowed against the EU budget, covering almost two-thirds of Ukraine’s estimated €70 billion financing gap for 2027 (FT, reposted by @F_CEAFE; LIGA.net).**

Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis had flagged the two-thirds target on 9 November. The previous €90 billion loan (December 2025) was backstopped by about €210 billion of immobilised Russian central-bank assets; Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic have opt-outs (Irish Times). Separately, Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen said she sent the Commission a letter asking for stronger EU-level action against crypto-assets used to finance Russia’s war and evade sanctions (Valtonen on X, RBC-Ukraine).
articles.why: Common borrowing is the EU acting at the scale no Member State reaches alone. Opt-outs and demands for exemptions weaken the very instrument that makes Europe credible. Closing crypto loopholes is the European side of the sanctions fight, which only works if it is applied at EU level.
articles.watch: Commission proposal (18 Nov); Belgian position on the Euroclear assets; next sanctions package. Political side: see World.

articles.headline: AI’s hidden materials: US-listed AXT booms on indium phosphide made in China
articles.summary:
**AXT Inc (Fremont, California), which makes gallium arsenide, indium phosphide (InP) and germanium substrates at plants in China, reported record Q3 revenue of $73.4 million, up 162% y/y, with InP revenue of $54.3 million (four times a year earlier) driven by optical connectivity for AI data centres (Semiconductor Today, 16 Nov).**

The order backlog grew from over $100 million to more than $500 million; Q4 guidance is about $90 million. AXT notes that shipments within China need no export licence, and its Chinese subsidiary Tongmei is raising up to $545 million and preparing a Hong Kong listing. Its Chinese joint venture JinMei supplies high-purity gallium and germanium, materials on which China imposes export controls.
articles.why: AI optics depend on a handful of compound-semiconductor substrate makers, with capacity concentrated in China. Europe’s Critical Raw Materials Act has to cover these niche materials (indium, gallium, germanium), or Europe’s photonics industry will remain exposed to export-control fights between Washington and Beijing.
articles.watch: Chinese gallium/germanium licensing; EU CRMA strategic projects in compound semiconductors.

articles.headline: EIC Accelerator backs 35 deep-tech firms, but 74 more lacked funding
articles.summary:
**The European Innovation Council selected 35 start-ups and SMEs from 453 full applications (88 interviews), with €84 million in proposed grants; 32 will be assessed for EIC Fund equity of up to €10 million each (EIC, 16 Nov).**

Companies come from 17 EU and associated countries, most from France, Switzerland and Germany; examples include DEESS (France, autonomous underwater seabed-mapping robots) and Ecobean (Poland). Another 74 proposals above the quality threshold received only a Seal of Excellence because funding ran out.
articles.why: 74 excellent projects without money is a measure of Europe’s funding gap, at a time when Washington finances its “national champions” (topic 1). It supports the case for a stronger FP10 and a European Competitiveness Fund (07:30 edition, topic 6).
articles.watch: FP10/MFF negotiations.

articles.headline: Nvidia crisis turns into a test of US export-control enforcement; Beijing calls the spy story a pretext
articles.summary:
**Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday, 12 November, after reports about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based data-centre firm Megaspeed whom US officials suspect of spying for China; Megaspeed is suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China in breach of US export controls.**

CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO. On Sunday, 15 November, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News that the board should look for an outside CEO, that Nvidia needed “a dramatic shake-up”, and that he wanted answers “in the next 10 days” on whether shell companies were used to sell restricted chips to China (CNBC, Axios, Al Jazeera). The Washington Post reported on 13 November an open clash between Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over why Commerce did not blacklist Megaspeed. A Reuters review published on 13 November found more than $3 billion (about 23 billion yuan) in Chinese computing projects specifying restricted Nvidia H100/H200/H800 processors; Reuters stresses the figure covers whole projects and does not prove delivery.

**China’s reaction (linked):** China’s Foreign Ministry called the “Chinese spy” claims “nothing but smears” (CCTV, 9–10 November) and on 12 November urged Washington to stop using spy narratives to justify technology restrictions (China Daily, Lianhe Zaobao; Chinese state media). No MOFCOM countermeasure has been reported yet; watch for one around the Trump–Xi–Putin meeting in Shenzhen on 19 November announced by China’s MFA.

**ALERT — not yet reposted by @F_CEAFE:** economic coercion/export-control story with an ASML reciprocity angle. Link: https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/15/us-treasury-chief-calls-for-outsider-to-lead-embattled-tech-firm-nvidia
articles.why: Washington is treating enforcement of its own chip controls as a matter of state, publicly steering the leadership of a private company. European firms such as ASML apply these US-driven restrictions on China, yet the EU imposes nothing reciprocal on the US even where it holds leverage (lithography). The episode also shows that US rules follow US hardware wherever it goes, an argument for European-designed compute and for the EU’s own export-control and screening tools rather than borrowed ones.
articles.watch: Nvidia Q3 results (18 Nov); board response to the 10-day deadline (~25 Nov); any Commerce listing of Megaspeed; Chinese countermeasures; NDAA chip amendments.

articles.headline: Oil heads back to surplus while US LNG exports hit records: Europe’s energy bill depends on others’ wars
articles.summary:
**The IEA’s November Oil Market Report says the world oil market is returning to surplus as Gulf exports recover: Gulf crude exports reached 15 mb/d in October, 82% of pre-war levels, inventories rose 52 mb in October and the agency expects a roughly 2 mb/d surplus in Q4 with a larger build in 2027.**

Goldman Sachs likewise sees a “sizeable surplus” in 2027 (about 2 mb/d, per Mint) even allowing for supply risks. Bloomberg reports US LNG exports at a fresh peak as new projects ramp up, easing shortages caused by the Middle East war. Supply risks remain: Zelensky said on 15 November Ukraine has disabled “more than 55%” of Russia’s oil-refining capacity (reposted by @F_CEAFE), and Yemen’s Houthis claimed drone strikes on pumping stations 5 and 6 of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline (claim by the Houthi military spokesman, reposted by @F_CEAFE; no independent confirmation found).
articles.why: Lower crude prices help European industry, but Europe’s gas balance increasingly runs through US LNG, the same supplier that asks Europe to buy its energy and weapons while practising energy nationalism itself. Diversifying suppliers and accelerating European generation is a sovereignty question, not only a price question.
articles.watch: US EIA STEO and IEA gas report; Brent reaction to Saudi pipeline claim; EU gas storage. Military side of the Gulf/Yemen war: see Conflicts.

articles.headline: Asia’s engines sputter: Japan contracts, China’s October data disappoint
articles.summary:
**Japan’s GDP fell an annualised 0.1% in July–September (−0.02% q/q), the first contraction in four quarters, against forecasts of growth; private consumption fell 0.3% while capital spending rose 1.6% on AI and labour-saving investment (Cabinet Office via Nikkei, Reuters, Kyodo, AP).**

Higher oil-import costs after the de facto closure of Hormuz in Q2 weighed on net exports (−0.6 pp). China’s October industrial output grew 4.8% y/y (5.5% in September), retail sales just 0.4%, and fixed-asset investment fell 8.1% in January–October, with property investment down 21.6% (National Bureau of Statistics). High-tech manufacturing grew 17.6% and semiconductor output 21.9% (NBS; ING).
articles.why: Weak Chinese domestic demand plus booming high-tech manufacturing and export deliveries (+18.6% y/y, ING) mean more Chinese overcapacity heading to third markets, including Europe. A common EU trade response, rather than 27 national ones, is the only scale that counts against it.
articles.watch: BoJ December meeting; China stimulus signals around APEC Shenzhen; Eurostat flash GDP/HICP releases this week.

articles.headline: “Economic Fury”: Washington predicts a 25% collapse of Iran’s economy
articles.summary:
**Treasury Secretary Bessent told Fox News on 15 November that Iran’s economy will contract by about 25% between March 2026 and March 2027 under US sanctions and the naval blockade, calling it “one of the fastest collapses in history” (Al Jazeera, Iran International).**

CENTCOM says the blockade has prevented more than $25 billion of Iranian crude exports (unverified), and Task Force Iron Gate, launched on 7 November, extends the pressure to land borders and the Caspian. A third US carrier, USS Theodore Roosevelt, entered CENTCOM’s area on 15 November (reposted by @F_CEAFE via Al Jazeera).
articles.why: US secondary sanctions decide which trade European firms may conduct with Iran, regardless of EU positions; the 2018 experience showed the EU blocking statute did not protect them. Europe pays in energy prices and in lost markets for a policy it does not set.
articles.watch: Iranian official response (Tasnim/IRNA Telegram, to be checked by Actualidad/Conflicts); oil-market effect. Military dimension: see Conflicts.

articles.headline: Nexperia: Wingtech appeals the Dutch Enterprise Chamber order (ongoing)
articles.summary:
**Wingtech said on 15 November it opposes the Amsterdam Enterprise Chamber’s latest interim order in the Nexperia dispute and will appeal, arguing it lacks a factual basis and contains fundamental legal flaws (Bloomberg, Reuters).**

Covered in detail in the 15 November R&D brief; no new Dutch or Chinese government step found since.
articles.why: Nexperia is a test of whether Europe can keep control of a strategic chipmaker using its own legal tools, and whether those tools are applied with the same rigour to US acquirers as to Chinese ones.
articles.watch: appeal filing in the Netherlands; MOFCOM statements; Nexperia China supply.

articles.headline: Poland at the G20: its claimed special relationship with the US vs. its real weight
articles.summary:
**Polish Deputy PM and Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote on 15 November that Poland’s GDP exceeds $1 trillion and that it has a seat at the G20 table. @F_CEAFE answered with the global rankings, where only a handful of Polish companies appear: 8 in the 2026 Forbes Global 2000, 1 among the world’s top 2,000 R&D investors (EU Industrial R&D Investment Scoreboard 2025) and 1 in the Defense News Top 100.**

These rankings are led first by US and then by Chinese companies; set against them, Poland’s presence is marginal, whatever its G20 aspirations or its claimed privileged relationship with Washington.
articles.why: It is CEAFE’s editorial line in figures: even the EU’s fastest-growing large economy lacks a base of global-scale companies and R&D investors. No member state alone carries real weight against the US and China; only European scale does.
articles.watch: The JRC 2026 R&D Scoreboard (December).

articles.headline: China turns its buying power on iron ore
articles.summary: **Australia’s Resources Minister Madeleine King said state-backed buyer China Mineral Resources Group’s use of purchasing power to push down iron-ore prices may breach international trade rules (Bloomberg, CNA, AFR).**
articles.why: A single state buyer gives China leverage that no fragmented market can match; Europe only negotiates on equal terms when it acts together.
articles.watch: Chinese reaction to Canberra’s remarks.

articles.headline: Wingtech says it will appeal Dutch Enterprise Chamber orders in the Nexperia dispute
articles.summary:
Wingtech Technology said in a filing to the Shanghai Stock Exchange on Sunday, 15 November 2026, that it will appeal an interim ruling of the Amsterdam Court of Appeal’s Enterprise Chamber (Ondernemingskamer) in the dispute over its chipmaking subsidiary Nexperia. The chamber, on 11 November, ordered additional immediate measures after concluding that actions by Wingtech and Nexperia China had undermined earlier rulings, according to Nexperia and contemporaneous reporting. The orders require Wingtech, founder Zhang Xuezheng, Nexperia China and others in Wingtech’s leadership to refrain from interfering with Nexperia’s normal business, respect the powers of independent court-appointed officials (including as they explore a possible long-term solution), permit market sounding with potential counterparties, withdraw specified claims filed in China, and not enforce certain measures of the Dongguan Intermediate People’s Court. Wingtech said the decision lacked a factual and legal basis, improperly interfered with ongoing Chinese proceedings, and amounted to a cross-border anti-suit injunction that deprived the controlling shareholder of its rights.

The wider dispute began when the Dutch state took control of Nexperia in September 2025 over concerns about possible technology transfer to Wingtech; the government later stepped back from that intervention in November 2025, but litigation has continued in both the Netherlands and China. Periodic penalty payments attached to the new orders are high; the judgment caps the total at €300 million. One withdrawal order carries €5 million per day of non-compliance, up to €100 million. A The Hague preliminary-relief judgment of 2 November 2026 had already ordered Nexperia China not to rely on a Jiangsu anti-suit injunction inside the EU, on pain of €1 million per day up to €100 million. Earlier in the enquiry procedure, the Enterprise Chamber found “well-founded reasons to doubt” proper management, suspended Zhang as CEO and transferred voting control of Wingtech’s Nexperia shares to a Dutch court-appointed lawyer.
articles.why: Nexperia is a major European source of essential semiconductor components for automotive and industrial customers. The case is a live test of Dutch and EU tools to ring-fence a sensitive chip asset from its Chinese parent, and of competing Chinese court orders. The outcome will bear on European supply-chain security, export-control policy and the credibility of economic-security interventions in the semiconductor sector.
articles.watch: Whether Wingtech actually files the Dutch appeal and withdraws the specified Chinese claims; any enforcement of the €300 million penalty cap; and whether court-appointed officials proceed with a “long-term solution,” including a possible change of control.

articles.headline: Australia signs a Horizon Europe association agreement; six new Regional Innovation Valleys launched
articles.summary:
The European Commission posted on Sunday that Australian researchers can now “join and lead projects” in Horizon Europe. Official pages confirm that a treaty-level association agreement was signed in Brussels on 12 November 2026 by Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation Ekaterina Zaharieva and Australia’s Minister for Industry and Innovation and Minister for Science, Tim Ayres. EURAXESS, citing Commission material, says association covers Horizon Europe’s €52.4 billion Pillar II (health, climate, energy, digital technologies and related areas); Australian entities will be able to join and lead consortia and access funding on similar terms to EU counterparts. Transitional arrangements from January 2027 will let Australian entities apply to Pillar II calls; formal completion is expected by mid-2027 after parliamentary scrutiny in Australia. Australia becomes the 24th country associated with Horizon Europe; the Commission also said negotiations with India were concluded on 6 November. Australia’s Department of Industry, Science and Resources lists shared interests including clean energy, critical minerals, advanced manufacturing, digital technologies, health, space and supply-chain security.

Separately, EISMEA reported that six new Regional Innovation Valleys projects were presented at a forum in Brussels on 12 November, forming a second wave under the 2025 Horizon Europe work programmes. They will receive nearly €43 million in Horizon Europe co-funding. The portfolio then totals 11 projects, about €190 million in total budget and a requested EU contribution of €95.2 million, with 182–183 partner participations across 18 member states and seven associated countries (26% of participations from widening countries). The six new projects are PIONEER and EQUIVALEMT (photonics and quantum), AGRITECHVALLEY (digital agriculture), MANUFACTURING RIV (circular and resilient manufacturing), VIVA (integrated ecosystems) and RIVAIRA (AI-driven regional acceleration). One hundred and forty-seven regions hold the RIV label. A “Selected Regional Innovation Valleys map” document is dated 11 November 2026; an updated interactive map is due in November.
articles.why: Association of a major Indo-Pacific partner to Pillar II, and a second wave of inter-regional innovation valleys in quantum, AI, agri-tech and manufacturing, are tools of economic security and of reducing the EU’s innovation divide — still modest in euro terms beside the scale of US and Chinese industrial policy.
articles.watch: Australian parliamentary treaty scrutiny and mid-2027 formal association; first 2027 Pillar II calls open to Australian coordinators; India association follow-through; kick-off of the six RIV projects and publication of the updated map.

articles.headline: GitHub Octoverse 2026: AI agents start more than 40% of pull requests
articles.summary:
GitHub used a short video on 14 November to recap its Octoverse 2026 report (published 28 October, updated 6 November). The report finds that by September 2026 more than 40% of pull requests on GitHub started from an AI agent’s first draft, up from 17% in March — 110 million agent-started pull requests in September alone, about six times March’s volume. Agent-started pull requests changed multiple files 87% of the time (versus 79% without detected agent involvement) and, by September, 90% were merged within two weeks. Among repositories created in 2026, those with an agent configuration file logged eight times as many commits as those without. GitHub defines an “agent-started” pull request as one whose first draft came from a detectable coding agent and calls that figure a floor.

Other headline numbers: 17.9 billion pushes and 34.3 billion commits in the year to 30 September 2026; more than 225 million developers, including 6.47 million in the United Kingdom, 6.30 million in Germany and 4.75 million in France. TypeScript remained the most-used language by contributors, ahead of Python and JavaScript. Fifty-five percent of monthly active Copilot users now use agentic features, up from 35% a year earlier.
articles.why: A large and rapidly growing share of software — including, in principle, code in defence, public-sector and critical-infrastructure repositories — is now first drafted by AI agents, mostly via US-hosted tools and models. That raises software-supply-chain, assurance, liability and dependency issues for European industry and governments. The geography of GitHub’s developer base, with three large EU communities in the global top ten, makes the shift a European phenomenon, not only a Silicon Valley one.
articles.watch: Any European Commission or ENISA guidance on AI-generated code in critical software; the share of agent-started pull requests in public defence- and government-related organisations; whether EU-hosted coding agents gain measurable share.

articles.headline: AMD EPYC 9996 (256 Zen 6C cores) begins shipping, with independent Linux benchmarks
articles.summary: AMD promoted a Phoronix review as 6th-generation EPYC 9006 “Venice” processors move from a July announcement to Socket SP7 availability, with systems beginning to ship from OEM/ODM partners. The flagship EPYC 9996 has 256 Zen 6C cores and 512 threads per socket (512 cores / 1,024 threads in a dual-socket configuration), a 2.55 GHz base and up to 4.1 GHz boost, 1,024 MB of L3 cache, a 600 W default TDP, 96 lanes of PCIe 6.0 and 16 memory channels of DDR5-8000 or MRDIMM-12800. List price is given as $14,904 per 1,000 units. AMD claims up to 2.2× the HPC performance of Intel’s Xeon 6980P. Phoronix editor Michael Larabel, writing on 10 November after hands-on tests on Ubuntu 26.10, called the part a “grand slam” and began publishing a multi-page Linux benchmark suite. Follow-on sockets and SKUs are due in 2027 (SP8 in the first half; 9006X and 9006LP “Verano” in the second half).
articles.why: Leading-edge CPU performance and memory bandwidth for HPC, AI training and defence-scale simulation remain concentrated in a small group of US firms. European institutional and industrial buyers will run this generation; the gap is relevant to EU efforts on sovereign HPC and chip design, and to the energy efficiency of large compute installations.
articles.watch: Remaining independent benchmarks; SP8 and Verano dates in 2027; any European HPC centre procurement announcements on the 9006 line.

articles.headline: Lutnick exigió al Gobierno de EE. UU. el 51 % de la start-up de baterías Pure Lithium, con 1.000 millones de dólares del compromiso inversor de Japón
articles.summary:
**El secretario de Comercio de EE. UU., Howard Lutnick, pidió en julio a la start-up de baterías Pure Lithium que cediera a Washington una participación de control del 51 % a cambio de financiar una planta que la empresa no poseería ni controlaría, según documentos y una fuente citados por Reuters el 20 de noviembre.**

La planta sería propiedad de un vehículo controlado por Tokio y Washington y se financiaría con 1.000 millones de dólares del compromiso japonés de invertir 550.000 millones en EE. UU. en el marco de su acuerdo arancelario; Pure Lithium solo la operaría y recibiría parte de los ingresos tras el servicio de la deuda. Lutnick dijo que el Gobierno necesitaba controlar la empresa para que su batería de litio metal pudiera usarla el ejército estadounidense. La empresa se negó («el 51 % está muy fuera de los precedentes e invita al escrutinio», escribió su bufete Skadden Arps el 22 de agosto) y Comercio rechazó su contraoferta del 9,9 %. @F_CEAFE compartió la exclusiva de Reuters a las 09:23 y una respuesta que recuerda que Pure Lithium trabaja con la canadiense E3 Lithium (09:24).

**Control de ALERTA de adquisiciones:** ninguna nueva compra de una empresa estratégica europea por una empresa o fondo estadounidense en esta ventana. @F_CEAFE ya ha publicado lo de Pure Lithium: sin ALERTA. Otras operaciones: KKR (EE. UU.) negocia una participación mayoritaria en EdgeCore Digital Infrastructure (centros de datos en EE. UU.) https://x.com/i/status/2123864009396940978 ; interés temprano de compra por el banco británico Metro Bank https://x.com/i/status/2123916845665120457

**Fuentes:** [reposts de @F_CEAFE](https://x.com/i/status/2124056146403016808), [original @Reuters](https://x.com/i/status/2123992347717329173), [original @Reuters](https://x.com/i/status/2124056255429849544), [· Reuters vía US News](https://money.usnews.com/investing/news/articles/2026-11-20/exclusive-lutnick-asked-battery-startup-pure-lithium-to-accept-us-takeover-documents-and-source-say), [· Investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/exclusivelutnick-asked-battery-startup-pure-lithium-to-accept-us-takeover-documents-and-source-say-5042851)
articles.why: Es política industrial mediante capital: Washington toma el control de una tecnología estratégica y un aliado (Japón) paga la fábrica con un compromiso de inversión ligado a los aranceles. La UE firmó su propio acuerdo arancelario con un compromiso de inversión en EE. UU.: debe esperar la misma palanca sobre ese dinero. La UE no tiene un instrumento equivalente a escala de la Unión.
articles.watch: Respuesta de Comercio; control del Congreso sobre las participaciones estatales; uso de los compromisos de Japón y de la UE.

articles.headline: Trump amenaza con un «impuesto tremendo» a las empresas de EE. UU. que construyan centros de datos de IA en el extranjero; «solo chips antiguos» para China
articles.summary:
**En su rueda de prensa del 20 de noviembre, el presidente Trump dijo que no se permitirá a las empresas estadounidenses construir centros de datos en otros países y que las que lo hagan afrontarán «un impuesto tremendo».**

No dio tipo, base legal ni fecha, y admitió que aún no se lo había dicho a su propio equipo (AP, CNBC, Axios). «Quien gane la superinteligencia, gana… No vamos a permitir que los centros de datos se vayan a otros países, porque China se quedará…», dijo. Sobre los chips para China: «Queremos solo chips antiguos, y no nos importa si no va ninguno». @F_CEAFE compartió estas declaraciones entre las 19:32 y las 20:48 del viernes. Al Jazeera y Bloomberg las vincularon el sábado con las restricciones de esta semana, que golpean a los centros de datos de Malasia, Singapur y Tailandia.

**Fuentes:** [reposts de @F_CEAFE](https://x.com/i/status/2123847020427284662), [reposts de @F_CEAFE](https://x.com/i/status/2123865998780432419), [reposts de @F_CEAFE](https://x.com/i/status/2123863207047578023), [· @AJEnglish](https://x.com/i/status/2124015156795699309), [· @business](https://x.com/i/status/2124108094783287541), [· @euronews](https://x.com/i/status/2123945122857361820), [· AP](https://apnews.com/article/trump-artificial-intelligence-data-centers-f1ac03b73d13445400eeed8631d9d879), [· CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/20/trump-data-centers-ai-companies-tax.html), [· Axios](https://www.axios.com/2026/11/20/us-ai-trump-data-centers-overseas), [· IBTimes UK](https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/trump-tax-ai-data-centres-abroad-legal-questions-1833720), [· Bloomberg Law](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/artificial-intelligence/asias-data-center-hotbed-hit-by-us-chip-curbs-as-trump-visits), [· MOFCOM 17 nov](https://www.mofcom.gov.cn/syxwfb/art/2026/art_3a69f2058b724dd39cd8ecddcaa4ab87.html)
articles.why: Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta y Oracle construyen buena parte de la capacidad de nube e IA de la UE. Un castigo a invertir fuera, sumado a la norma del BIS sobre acceso remoto del 16 de noviembre que ya cubre los centros de datos de la UE, haría depender la capacidad de cálculo europea del permiso y los impuestos de Washington. Es el doble rasero de EE. UU.: «América primero» para su infraestructura y mercados abiertos exigidos a los demás. La lección: cálculo y nube soberanos europeos, como empiezan a apuntar las nuevas normas españolas sobre centros de datos.
articles.watch: Posible orden ejecutiva o proyecto de ley; reacción de Bruselas y de las capitales con proyectos de hiperescala; contramedidas del MOFCOM.

articles.headline: La «Operación Economic Outcast» de la OFAC apunta a los «fideicomisarios del petróleo» de Irán; el Tesoro presiona a Singapur y Malasia; Teherán habla de una «guerra económica silenciosa»
articles.summary:
**El 20 de noviembre la OFAC sancionó a cuatro iraníes: Mohammad Javad Bavand, exoficial de inteligencia de la Guardia Revolucionaria, y Majid Taj, acusados de recuperar ingresos petroleros iraníes depositados en terceros países (E.O.**

13902), y Mohammadhossein Servati y Mojtaba Arabnejad, vinculados a la empresa pantalla Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars y a Mahan Air (E.O. 13224). El Tesoro afirma que «no hay petróleo en el mar fuera del bloqueo militar de EE. UU.» y que el régimen «quizá nunca vea los ingresos del petróleo que ya ha vendido» (Bessent). Ese mismo día, funcionarios del Tesoro advirtieron a los reguladores de Singapur y Malasia de los riesgos de no aplicar las sanciones de EE. UU. a Irán; Singapur dijo que refuerza sus salvaguardias y Malasia no respondió (Reuters). Reacción: el presidente Pezeshkian afirmó que Irán sufre una «guerra económica silenciosa» «más dura que una guerra con misiles» (Al Jazeera, citando a medios estatales iraníes). @F_CEAFE compartió los mensajes del Tesoro y de Bessent (00:18–01:55 del sábado).

**Fuentes:** [reposts de @F_CEAFE](https://x.com/i/status/2123918858167742844), [reposts de @F_CEAFE](https://x.com/i/status/2123920605322121330), [reposts de @F_CEAFE](https://x.com/i/status/2123943226113499252), [· @Reuters](https://x.com/i/status/2123854076022575489), [· @AJEnglish](https://x.com/i/status/2124065050000519666), [· @AJEnglish](https://x.com/i/status/2123950026418475324), [· @AJEnglish](https://x.com/i/status/2124085991480955377), [· Tesoro](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0697), [· OFAC](https://ofac.treasury.gov/recent-actions/20261120), [· Reuters vía FMT](https://www.freemalaysiatoday.com/category/highlight/2026/11/20/us-treasury-presses-singapore-malaysia-on-iran-sanctions-compliance)
articles.why: El Tesoro dice trabajar «con socios… la Unión Europea, el Reino Unido, socios del Golfo» y haber «ampliado la exposición a sanciones de personas no estadounidenses». Bancos, navieras y aseguradoras europeos quedan sujetos a sanciones secundarias de EE. UU. lo acuerde o no la UE: el núcleo del problema de la extraterritorialidad. Bessent citó además un «consenso entre EE. UU., Rusia y China en Shenzhen» sobre el suministro de petróleo: las grandes potencias ordenan el mercado energético entre ellas y Europa acepta precios.
articles.watch: Respuesta china sobre las refinerías; posición de la UE; precios del crudo.

articles.headline: La UE ultima «ReadyEU», un instrumento para cerrar con rapidez el acceso a su mercado; Pekín alerta de «proteccionismo institucionalizado»
articles.summary:
**La UE ultima un nuevo instrumento, provisionalmente «ReadyEU», que permitiría a la Comisión Europea bloquear con rapidez bienes y servicios concretos en el mercado único de 450 millones de consumidores, según Bloomberg (20 de noviembre).**

Podría activarse si un país interfiere en las decisiones comerciales de la UE, incumple las normas de la OMC o de un acuerdo comercial y se niega a resolverlo, o ante una amenaza económica inmediata y grave. Forma parte de un paquete para reducir el déficit comercial de la UE con China (360.000 millones de euros en 2025), con instrumentos de defensa comercial más flexibles y un mecanismo de diversificación en sectores estratégicos, que se presentará el 9 de diciembre, antes del Consejo Europeo del 17–18 de diciembre. Reacción: Global Times (medio estatal chino), citando a analistas chinos, dice que el «proteccionismo institucionalizado» encarecerá los costes de las empresas europeas sin devolver la fuerza industrial.

**Fuentes:** [@business](https://x.com/i/status/2123926903140602034), [· @globaltimesnews](https://x.com/i/status/2124069971353583774), [· repost de @F_CEAFE](https://x.com/i/status/2123860618583110114), [· Bloomberg vía Bloomberg TV Bulgaria](https://www.bloombergtv.bg/a/2-novini/167227-es-e-blizo-do-nov-instrument-za-blokirane-na-dostapa-do-edinniya-pazar), [· Global Times](https://www.globaltimes.cn/page/202611/1374757.shtml), [· Politico](https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-commission-eyes-rule-change-to-retaliate-faster-against-china/)
articles.why: Responde a la crítica de CEAFE sobre la falta de reciprocidad europea ante la coerción económica. Según Politico, haría falta una mayoría cualificada de Estados miembros de la UE para bloquear su uso, un listón mucho más bajo que el del Instrumento contra la Coerción, nunca utilizado. No va dirigido a un país concreto, por lo que también serviría frente a la coerción estadounidense (amenazas sobre Groenlandia en enero).
articles.watch: Paquete del 9 de diciembre; reacción del MOFCOM; negociaciones UE–China sobre química y maquinaria (enero y marzo).

articles.headline: La segunda crisis energética de Europa llega al mercado eléctrico: acerías que paran en las horas caras
articles.summary:
**Bloomberg (21 de noviembre) informa de que la segunda gran crisis energética europea en menos de cinco años ya se nota en la electricidad mayorista: los contratos para cada uno de los próximos tres meses cotizan en torno a 200 €/MWh, aproximadamente el doble que el invierno pasado, porque el gas europeo se ha triplicado en un año al tensarse el suministro mundial por la guerra de Oriente Medio.**

Una acería alemana del grupo italiano Feralpi para en las horas caras pese a tener pedidos. Dos comercializadoras alemanas, Grüüün y Stromee, dejaron de suministrar; la austriaca Verbund sufrió un impacto de 120 millones de euros y la española Acerinox de 16 millones en un trimestre. En un escenario severo, los contratos mensuales podrían llegar a 300 €/MWh (BB Energy).

**Fuentes:** [@business](https://x.com/i/status/2124067828487598317), [@business](https://x.com/i/status/2123949571457888570), [@business](https://x.com/i/status/2123845110869700796), [· @euronews](https://x.com/i/status/2123911510884041197), [· Bloomberg vía Energy Connects](https://www.energyconnects.com/news/utilities/2026/november/europe-s-power-market-is-flashing-a-warning-to-its-economy/)
articles.why: Es la línea energética de CEAFE: el gas caro empuja a la industria intensiva en energía a parar o deslocalizarse, mientras Europa ha cambiado la dependencia del gas ruso por la del GNL estadounidense (P-TEC, 18 de noviembre). Alemania prepara la vuelta de centrales de carbón y fuel de la reserva.
articles.watch: Futuros de TTF y electricidad; ley alemana de reserva; reunión del BCE del 17 de diciembre.

articles.headline: Mercedes-Benz, a punto de quedar atrapada por la prohibición de coches chinos en EE. UU. por sus accionistas chinos
articles.summary:
**Los legisladores de EE. UU. están cerca de un acuerdo sobre una ley que prohibiría los coches chinos en su mercado, tras negociaciones de última hora destinadas en parte a salvar a Mercedes-Benz, cuyo capital está en casi un 20 % en manos de entidades chinas, por encima del umbral propuesto del 15 % (Bloomberg Law, WSJ).**

La solución negociada exime las participaciones chinas pasivas sin derecho de voto. Sus promotores, de estados productores de automóviles, quieren llevar la ley a Trump antes de fin de año.

**Fuentes:** [@WSJ](https://x.com/i/status/2123940249432739868), [· Bloomberg Law](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/international-trade/us-lawmakers-near-deal-to-ban-chinese-cars-in-lame-duck-session)
articles.why: El acceso de un campeón europeo al mercado de EE. UU. depende de que el Congreso redacte una excepción: la rivalidad EE. UU.–China se convierte en normas sobre el accionariado de las empresas europeas. También muestra el riesgo de las participaciones chinas en empresas estratégicas europeas.
articles.watch: Texto final; exposición de Daimler Truck, BMW y proveedores; reacción del Gobierno alemán.

articles.headline: Acuerdos comerciales de EE. UU. ligados a compras de energía: Tailandia, Filipinas, México
articles.summary:
**Trump anunció acuerdos comerciales con Tailandia (que elimina aranceles al 99 % de las exportaciones de EE. UU. y comprará 2.600 millones de dólares más en productos agrícolas estadounidenses) y Filipinas, y dijo que el acuerdo con México está cerca y el de Canadá, más atrasado (Bloomberg).**

Sobre su conversación con el presidente filipino Marcos: «¿Dónde compran su energía?» «En Oriente Medio.» «Ya no. Van a comprar el 100 % de su energía…» a EE. UU. @F_CEAFE compartió ambos vídeos (20:38–20:45 del viernes).

**Fuentes:** [reposts de @F_CEAFE](https://x.com/i/status/2123863584178622840), [reposts de @F_CEAFE](https://x.com/i/status/2123865421493207425), [· @business](https://x.com/i/status/2123892929643094283)
