articles.headline: Washington presses ahead with a ban on Chinese optical transceivers for US data centres, over the objections of its own tech giants
articles.summary:
The Trump administration plans to press ahead with a Federal Communications Commission (FCC) measure that would block US imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers, the components that carry data over fibre-optic cables inside data centres, Reuters reported in an exclusive picked up by its tech desk this morning. Amazon, Google, Meta, CoreWeave and Cisco joined Microsoft in lobbying White House officials against it, warning that compliance could take up to a decade; three people familiar with the matter say it is moving forward anyway, though it could still be shelved. China holds two-thirds of the global market (Counterpoint Research), led by Eoptolink and Zhongji Innolight, which is on the Pentagon’s list of Chinese military-linked companies; US makers Coherent and Lumentum lack the scale to replace them. US firms raised the risk that Beijing retaliates by banning exports of indium phosphide, a critical mineral needed to make transceivers. The same morning Singapore’s prime minister, Lawrence Wong, said the new US chip rules will cut the volume of high-end chips transshipped through the city-state, that Singapore is “not here to implement or enforce the export controls of other countries”, but that it will facilitate US checks on chips deployed locally.

**Linked action–reaction:** FCC bans on new Chinese drones, robots, power inverters and routers over the past year → transceiver ban drafted (August, Reuters) → pushed ahead despite lobbying (17–18 November). **China’s response:** the Chinese Embassy in Washington said Beijing “firmly opposes the US overstretching the concept of national security”, urged Washington to “stop smearing Chinese companies and threatening them with sanctions”, and said China “will continue to do what is necessary to firmly defend the legitimate and lawful rights and interests of Chinese companies” (quoted by Reuters). No MOFCOM statement found yet; the MFA’s 18 November briefing did not address it.

**Key facts.**

- Measure: FCC ban on US imports of *new models* of Chinese optical transceivers; no implementation date or exemptions announced (Reuters via Investing.com; Bloomberg Law).

- Market: China about two-thirds of global supply (Counterpoint); Coherent +2.2% and Lumentum +1.5% after the report.

- Singapore (CNA, 18 Nov): most chips recorded as sales to Singapore are transshipped; firms using Singapore to circumvent controls face “clear and firm action”. ASEAN also agreed to China’s proposal to make 2027 the Year of ASEAN-China AI Cooperation.

- Malaysia’s Q3 growth was revised up on AI demand while officials gauge the impact of the new US rules (Bloomberg).

**Sources:** [@ReutersTech](https://x.com/i/status/2122984414472810567), [Reuters via Investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/exclusivetrumps-china-data-center-curb-advances-despite-amazon-google-meta-lobbying-5032280), [Bloomberg Law](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/artificial-intelligence/us-to-push-ahead-on-china-data-center-tech-import-ban-rtrs-1), [CNA](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/singapore/ai-chips-us-lawrence-wong-donald-trump-6560086), [@business (Singapore)](https://x.com/i/status/2122965576410599635), [@business (Malaysia)](https://x.com/i/status/2122942928574107959)
articles.why: Washington is willing to impose a ten-year adjustment cost on its own champions to remove Chinese hardware from its data centres, and asks transit hubs such as Singapore to police chip flows. The same logic is applied to Europe through the remote-access rule (16 November), which covers data centres in the EU. Europe has no comparable policy of its own on who supplies the physical layer of its AI infrastructure; it either follows Washington’s list or does nothing. A European screening and supply policy (European suppliers first, decided in Brussels, not copied from the FCC) is the condition for autonomy rather than alignment.
articles.watch: FCC publication and any exemptions; MOFCOM reaction and whether Beijing restricts indium phosphide; whether the EU or member states adopt similar bans.

articles.headline: Update: Beijing answers Nvidia’s China halt with one line, while Chinese chipmakers post record results
articles.summary:
Asked by AFP about Nvidia’s halt of licensed Hopper (H200) shipments to China, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said only: “We have made clear more than once our principled position on U.S. chip exports to China.” Global Times (Chinese state media) set the halt against a run of record quarterly results from Chinese chipmakers, which it says shows US export controls are accelerating self-sufficiency. Memory maker CXMT reported third-quarter revenue of 118.71 billion yuan ($17.8 billion), up 613.2% year on year; GPU designers MetaX (1.5 billion yuan, +367%) and Moore Threads (1.55 billion yuan, +1,773.92%) also posted records, and SMIC’s revenue reached a record $3.19 billion. Citing IDC, the paper says Nvidia’s share of China’s data-centre AI-chip market fell to 34% in the first half of 2026, against 28% for Huawei.

**Linked action–reaction:** BIS remote-access rule (16 Nov) → MFA and MOFCOM threaten countermeasures (17 Nov) → Nvidia stops licensed sales to China (17 Nov, US time) → MFA restates its “principled position” (18 Nov); MOFCOM has not commented on the halt (its spokesperson pages did not render).

**Key facts.**

- Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators in China in January–June 2026 (−44%), Huawei 572,000 (IDC, via Global Times).

- TrendForce forecasts Chinese high-end AI-chip shipments of 5 million units in 2026 (+83%) (via Global Times).

- In Washington, Democratic lawmakers opened a probe into whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick helped Cantor Fitzgerald, controlled by his sons, avoid losses linked to the Nvidia scandal (FT, via Reuters).

**Sources:** [China MFA (18 Nov briefing)](https://www.fmprc.gov.cn/eng/xw/fyrbt/lxjzh/202611/t20261118_12062001.html), [Global Times (Chinese state media)](https://www.globaltimes.cn/page/202611/1374545.shtml), [@globaltimesnews (Chinese state media)](https://x.com/i/status/2122955913565028557), [@globaltimesnews (chipmakers)](https://x.com/i/status/2123000783192961401), [@Reuters (Lutnick probe)](https://x.com/i/status/2123004583601463335), [@ReutersTech (Nvidia succession)](https://x.com/i/status/2122984410861518866), [@Reuters](https://x.com/i/status/2122985740917203327)
articles.why: Export controls built to slow China are instead consolidating a Chinese chip industry with its own domestic market, while the US keeps supply of advanced AI chips (Global Times cites a think-tank estimate of 94% US supply in the first half of 2026). Europe has neither of the two positions: it is not a supplier of AI accelerators at scale, and it accepts US rules for its own data centres. What these figures reveal is an asymmetry of power, not a difference in talent.
articles.watch: The Trump–Xi–Putin meeting in Shenzhen; the 1 December House hearing with Jensen Huang; MOFCOM.

articles.headline: Bloomberg finds US screening of Chinese investment has widened well beyond sensitive tech, even as Trump courts Chinese capital
articles.summary:
A Bloomberg News analysis of 137 deals that faced US security review shows the obstacles to Chinese investment have multiplied and now go beyond sensitive technology companies, undercutting President Trump’s effort to reopen the door to Chinese capital. The report (17 November, by Lucille Liu, Nectar Gan, Jenny Leonard and others) is paywalled; its headline findings were carried by Bloomberg’s X account and by aggregators. In May, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spoke of a US–China “Board of Investment” to fast-track deals in non-sensitive areas (Bloomberg).

**Key facts.**

- Sample: 137 deals reviewed by US security panels (Bloomberg).

- Finding: barriers now reach beyond sensitive tech (Bloomberg; details behind paywall).

**Sources:** [@business](https://x.com/i/status/2122969852306477124), [Bloomberg (via NewsAgent Data)](https://newsagentdata.com/news/a/1050286289-trump-s-push-to-reopen-us-doors-to-chinese-investment-faces), [Bloomberg (Bessent, May 2026)](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-05-14/bessent-says-us-china-are-discussing-a-board-of-investment)
articles.why: The US keeps control over who buys what on its soil, through CFIUS, sector bans and ownership rules for defence and strategic firms, even when the president wants the money. Europe applies US-inspired limits to Chinese buyers but has no equivalent screening of US purchases of its own strategic companies. The FDI Screening Regulation could provide the same reciprocity if it were used as Washington uses CFIUS. **Takeover alert check:** no new purchase of a European strategic firm by a US buyer was found in this window.
articles.watch: Whether the Shenzhen summit produces an investment mechanism; CFIUS decisions on European deals (ICEYE–Avio, see Defence Industry).

articles.headline: Uniper’s workers warn Centrica and Equinor off a takeover of Germany’s state-owned gas importer
articles.summary:
Uniper’s works council stepped up its opposition to a sale of the German state-owned utility, directly warning suitors including Britain’s Centrica and Norway’s Equinor not to pursue a takeover against the will of employees (Bloomberg). Works-council chair Martin Geilhorn said a stock-market listing is “the best solution for the employees, for the company and for stakeholders in Germany” and urged the federal finance ministry and North Rhine-Westphalia to resist takeover attempts. Centrica, Equinor and a consortium of Canada’s Brookfield Asset Management and Canada Pension Plan Investment Board advanced to the second round, while Czech EPH and a KKR–RWE consortium were eliminated (Bloomberg, 14 November). Berlin, which took control in the 2022 gas crisis with a €13.5 billion bailout, wants to keep about 25% after any deal.

**Key facts.**

- Market capitalisation nearly €18 billion; an IPO might value Uniper at about €12 billion, and any sale would likely be well below market value (Bloomberg; Headliner).

- Germany intends to retain around 25% after a transaction.

- German co-determination gives worker representatives strong influence over takeovers.

**Sources:** [@business](https://x.com/i/status/2122968091403362499), [Headliner (Bloomberg)](https://www.headliner.nl/artikelen/ondernemingsraad-uniper-waarschuwt-centrica-equinor-vijandig-overnamebod-258474), [Energy Connects (Bloomberg)](https://www.energyconnects.com/news/utilities/2026/november/centrica-equinor-in-next-round-of-germany-s-uniper-sale/), [Morningstar (Alliance News)](https://www.morningstar.com/news/alliance-news/1794648037338228300/press-equinor-and-centrica-still-in-running-to-buy-uniper-bloomberg)
articles.why: Uniper is one of Germany’s largest gas importers and power producers, so its owner matters for European energy security. A European buyer (Centrica or the majority state-owned Equinor) would keep it in European hands; the Brookfield–CPPIB consortium would put a critical energy asset under North American financial control. The US fund KKR is already out. Germany’s choice will show whether energy security is treated as strategic or simply sold to the highest bidder.
articles.watch: Second-round bids and timing; the BASF–Evonik bid (07:30 edition) and Berlin’s new takeover law (17 November) as the other German tests.

articles.headline: China doubles a 20-year US LNG contract with Venture Global as Trump lands in Shenzhen, and Asia competes with Europe for US gas
articles.summary:
China Gas Holdings and US exporter Venture Global signed, on the sidelines of the APEC CEO Summit, an agreement for 1.0 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) of US LNG for 20 years from 2030, doubling a 0.5 MTPA deal signed in September. The FOB contract is priced off Henry Hub plus a fixed liquefaction fee, and lifts China Gas’s long-term commitments with Venture Global to 3.0 MTPA (4 MTPA across all its suppliers). Chinese buyers had stopped importing US LNG in March 2025 after Beijing put tariffs on US energy (Reuters via Boursorama). Meanwhile, Brent hovered near $93 a barrel as tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz (a gas tanker abandoned after being hit, an ADNOC vessel attacked with 11 crew injured) were offset by forecasts of a supply surplus and higher US crude stocks.

**Key facts.**

- Seller: Venture Global (Arlington, US; Calcasieu Pass, Plaquemines and CP2 LNG in Louisiana). Buyer: China Gas Holdings (Hong Kong-listed, 0384.HK).

- Deliveries from 2030; price not disclosed.

- Brent around $92.6–93.1 on 18 November (Economic Times, CNBC).

**Sources:** [Venture Global](https://investors.ventureglobal.com/news/news-details/2026/Venture-Global-and-China-Gas-Announce-Increased-Long-Term-LNG-Agreement/default.aspx), [China Gas](https://www.chinagasholdings.com/news_view.aspx?Fid=t2%3A4%3A2&Id=4536&TypeId=4), [Reuters via Boursorama](https://www.boursorama.com/bourse/actualites/china-gas-double-le-volume-de-son-contrat-de-gnl-d-une-duree-de-20-ans-conclu-avec-venture-global-19cfaac5e6edb446fbbd1ccee22bd52d), [elEconomista](https://www.eleconomista.es/energia/noticias/14028694/11/26/china-recibe-a-trump-con-un-acuerdo-millonario-para-la-compra-de-gas-a-eeuu.html), [@Reuters](https://x.com/i/status/2122965581699621325), [@Reuters (Hormuz tanker)](https://x.com/i/status/2122998284893536415), [@AJEnglish (ADNOC)](https://x.com/i/status/2122954637150236892), [Economic Times](https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/markets/commodities/news/oil-price-today-november-18-brent-crude-drops-below-93-as-traders-weigh-supply-surplus-and-fresh-attacks-what-are-experts-saying/articleshow/135945687.cms), [@Reuters (QatarEnergy)](https://x.com/i/status/2123002060337492160)
articles.why: US gas is now Europe’s main alternative to Russian supply, at a price the US Interior Secretary says is 11 times the US price (07:30 edition). Long-term Chinese contracts from the same Louisiana plants show that Washington sells to Beijing what it urges Europe to buy instead of Russian gas, and that Asia will compete for those cargoes (elEconomista). Energy dependence has simply moved from one supplier to another.
articles.watch: Further US–China energy deals at the summit; EU gas storage and TTF; QatarEnergy’s expansion.

articles.headline: Euro-area inflation confirmed at 4.0% in October, with energy prices up 21%
articles.summary:
Eurostat confirmed euro-area annual inflation at 4.0% in October 2026, up from 3.8% in September and 2.1% a year earlier; EU inflation was also 4.0%. Energy prices rose 21.0% year on year (revised up from the 20.8% flash estimate) and contributed 1.89 percentage points, almost half of the total. Rates ranged from 0.6% in Sweden to 7.0% in Romania; Italy jumped to 5.6% (from 4.2%) and Spain stood at 4.9%. UK inflation rose to its highest level in a year after a surge in energy bills and motor fuel costs (Bloomberg, Reuters). In Berlin, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s coalition agreed after overnight talks to cut the electricity tax by about two cents to 0.1 cents per kWh for households and small businesses from January to December 2027, and to cap fuel prices from January, initially for three months (AFP). AFP links the surge in German energy costs to the US-Israeli war against Iran and the disruption of shipping through Hormuz.

**Key facts.**

- Euro area, October 2026: all-items 4.0%; excluding energy 2.3%; services 3.3%; monthly rate 0.5% (Eurostat).

- Highest: Romania 7.0%, Lithuania 6.1%, Bulgaria 5.9%; lowest: Sweden 0.6%, Czechia and Denmark 2.1%. Germany 2.9%, France 3.7%, Poland 3.7%.

- Next flash estimate (November): 1 December 2026.

- German cut: average household saving about €50 a year, based on 2,400 kWh consumption (AFP, citing BDEW); until now only some heavy industries had a reduction.

**Sources:** [Eurostat](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-euro-indicators/w/2-18112026-ap), [@business (UK inflation)](https://x.com/i/status/2122994508572856523), [@Reuters (UK)](https://x.com/i/status/2122988232828760250), [@business (Germany)](https://x.com/i/status/2122997026879050112), [AFP](https://www.afp.com/en/germany-cut-electricity-tax-cap-fuel-prices), [European Commission (autumn forecast)](https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/economic-forecast-and-surveys/economic-forecasts/autumn-2026-economic-forecast-shows-continued-growth-amid-higher-inflation_en)
articles.why: Energy is again the main driver of European inflation, and each government is answering on its own, with temporary national tax cuts. The Commission’s autumn forecast (17 November) already put euro-area inflation at 3.2% for 2026 and France’s growth at 0.4%. Without a common energy policy and its own supply, the EU pays the price of others’ wars and contracts.
articles.watch: ECB reaction; November flash estimate (1 December); EU-level energy measures.

articles.headline: Update: Nvidia stops shipping its US-licensed Hopper chips to China, two days after Washington’s remote-access rule
articles.summary:
**Nvidia’s interim chief executive, Colette Kress, told analysts on 17 November (US time) that the company is “no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China” and that its guidance “does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included”.**

Nvidia sold $2.4 billion of those licensed chips (the H200, approved for China by President Trump last year in a deal brokered by Jensen Huang, routed through the US with a 25% levy) in the third quarter. She gave no reason. TechCrunch, citing Georgetown’s CSET, notes that Beijing had already largely refused to accept H200 deliveries, preferring to build demand for Chinese chips. The same call brought record results: revenue of $115.8 billion (+103% year on year), data-centre revenue of $107.6 billion and a Q4 forecast of $130 billion ±3%. The board chair, Harvey Jones, said Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”. Separately, the WSJ reported that the SEC is investigating Nvidia, and a Microsoft executive told Bloomberg that the turmoil could push customers towards rival chips.

**Linked action–reaction:** US Commerce/BIS rule on remote access to advanced AI chips (16 November) → China’s MFA calls it “economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction” and MOFCOM threatens countermeasures (17 November; 20:30 edition) → Nvidia halts its remaining licensed China sales (17 November, US time). **China’s response to the halt: none found yet** on the MOFCOM and MFA sites; Global Times (Chinese state media) framed the results against “Washington tightening restrictions on advanced chips”. Watch the MFA briefing today (Beijing afternoon).

**Sources:** [Bloomberg Law](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/international-trade/nvidia-stops-selling-ai-chips-to-china-despite-us-approval), [Business Standard](https://www.business-standard.com/world-news/nvidia-stops-shipping-hopper-ai-chips-to-china-despite-us-approval-126111800204_1.html), [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/17/nvidia-is-abandoning-china-after-jensen-huangs-ouster/), [@business](https://x.com/i/status/2122882390510964817), [X](https://x.com/i/status/2122832200475283825), [X](https://x.com/i/status/2122796879725363307), [X](https://x.com/i/status/2122825237431480364), [X](https://x.com/i/status/2122894848806236342), [@ReutersTech](https://x.com/i/status/2122873274564485559), [X](https://x.com/i/status/2122853628436164666)
articles.why: The chip market is now set by a US rule, a US company’s board and Beijing’s purchasing policy; Europe has a say in none of them, even though the remote-access rule also covers data centres in the EU. Europe’s fastest supercomputer, JUPITER (EuroHPC/Jülich), runs on NVIDIA GH200 chips (TOP500, November 2026), so a supplier whose sales are now openly tied to US national-security oversight is a dependency, not a neutral vendor. Jefferies estimates the remote-access rule could cut $44–62 billion from Nvidia’s data-centre revenue next year (TechCrunch); Kress says the backlog means no top-line impact. What these figures reveal is an asymmetry of power, not a difference in talent or political will.
articles.watch: MFA and MOFCOM reaction; whether the halt is formalised as a licence change by BIS; the 1 December hearing; the Trump–Xi meeting in Shenzhen.

articles.headline: AMD completes its $2.9 billion purchase of Canada’s Taalas, another allied chip start-up absorbed by a US giant
articles.summary:
**AMD (Santa Clara, US) announced on 17 November that it has completed the acquisition of Taalas (Toronto, Canada), a designer of AI inference chips built for specific models (its first chip was tailored to Meta’s Llama).**

AMD will put Taalas’ technology into its accelerator roadmap alongside its Instinct GPUs. In a filing on 4 November AMD valued the cash-and-stock deal at about $2.9 billion, of which $1.4 billion is contingent. The Globe and Mail calls it one of the largest takeovers of a Canadian tech company, after Ecolab’s $4.75 billion purchase of CoolIT this year. Taalas, founded in 2023 by former AMD engineers, had raised over $225 million and had 24 employees in February; its implied valuation in November 2025 was over $750 million. AMD also bought San Francisco’s World Labs for $8.2 billion in September and hired the engineers of Toronto’s Untether in 2025.

**Sources:** [AMD](https://newsroom.amd.com/news/amd-completes-acquisition-taalas-advance-ai-inference-innovation/), [The Globe and Mail](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/business/article-amd-to-pay-29-billion-for-ai-chip-firm-taalas/), [EQT](https://eqtgroup.com/news/eqt-to-acquire-flatiron-energy-a-leading-developer-and-operator-of-battery-energy-storage-in-the-eastern-us-2026-11-17)
articles.why: This is the pattern CEAFE tracks. A promising chip start-up in an allied country grows on local talent and venture money and then ends up inside a US group, so its technology and intellectual property answer to US decisions, including export controls. Europe’s start-ups face the same pull: the Atomico report published today puts US start-up funding at $450 billion this year against $81 billion in Europe. no new purchase of a European strategic firm by a US buyer was reported since the previous edition. The opposite flow did happen: Sweden’s EQT agreed to buy Flatiron Energy, a US battery-storage developer with a 24 GWh portfolio (closing expected Q4 2026).
articles.watch: AMD’s integration plans; Canadian investment-review debate; any US bid for European chip or AI start-ups (Helsing, Neura Robotics and Quantum Systems have each raised more than $1 billion recently, per Atomico).

articles.headline: BASF readies a new bid for Evonik, offering job and site guarantees to win over Berlin and Düsseldorf
articles.summary:
**BASF is preparing another offer for its German peer Evonik, after Evonik rejected a sweetened bid worth more than €11 billion (€24 a share), Bloomberg and Reuters reported on 17 November.**

In a draft letter to the North Rhine-Westphalia government, members of the Bundestag and the RAG Foundation, Evonik’s largest shareholder with about 43%, BASF offers to rule out layoffs for a period still to be set, keep all German production sites and invest in R&D and greener production. The amounts and years are left as placeholders. “In a combined company, existing commitments to employees and sites will be honored and expanded,” the letter says. A new offer could come within days. NRW’s government repeated that Evonik’s independence should be protected, and Evonik’s top labour representative said BASF’s pledges offered “no additional value” if they merely restate existing protections. In October BASF’s CEO Markus Kamieth promised to honour Evonik’s employment guarantees until 2032 and to keep running the Marl and Wesseling chemical parks (about 3,500 jobs), which Evonik plans to sell.

**Sources:** [live.euronext.com](https://live.euronext.com/en/financial-news/basf-considers-further-concessions-bid-evonik-sources-say), [MarketScreener](https://ca.marketscreener.com/news/insider-basf-makes-another-push-at-evonik-with-further-concessions-ce785edcdd8bfe23), [investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/evonik-shares-rise-on-report-basf-prepares-renewed-takeover-offer-5033438), [BASF](https://www.basf.com/global/en/evonik), [@business](https://x.com/i/status/2122877500799746119)
articles.why: A European consolidation in a strategic industry, chemicals, that is under pressure from energy prices far above those in the US and from Chinese overcapacity. A larger European champion is in line with the scale argument CEAFE makes. The test is whether it brings investment rather than closures, which is what the regional government and the unions are now negotiating. It follows Berlin’s plans to overhaul takeover law after UniCredit–Commerzbank (20:30 edition).
articles.watch: The new offer price; RAG Foundation board decision; whether Berlin’s new takeover rules apply.

articles.headline: Washington sells its LNG in Warsaw and Manila, as US officials boast that Europe pays 11 times the American gas price
articles.summary:
**US Energy Secretary Chris Wright arrived in Warsaw on 17 November (“Great to be back in Warsaw for P-TEC”) for the seventh Partnership for Transatlantic Energy Cooperation, co-organised by the US Department of Energy, the Atlantic Council and Poland’s Ministry of Energy: a business forum today (18 November) and a ministerial meeting tomorrow, with sessions on long-term LNG supply security, transatlantic LNG and civil nuclear cooperation.**

EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen and the deputy prime ministers of Czechia, Slovakia and Hungary are among the invited guests. Wright wrote that “together with our European allies” Washington is working to “unleash energy abundance”. And now, with our new main supplier, gas prices in Europe are 11 times higher than in the US.” He illustrated it with an October chart by US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum comparing Henry Hub with Europe’s TTF and Asia’s JKM. The same evening, in Manila, President Trump said that “thanks to a historic investment from South Korea, we also just approved a colossal liquefied natural gas pipeline in Alaska”. Yonhap notes the White House has tied $54 billion to the project, while Seoul says its participation is still subject to a commercial-viability review, and that Trump had threatened to “charge them more” if Korea did not invest.

**Sources:** [gov.pl](https://www.gov.pl/web/energia/p-tec-w-warszawie-polska-w-centrum-transatlantyckiego-dialogu-o-bezpieczenstwie-energetycznym), [@SecretaryWright](https://x.com/i/status/2122746320259584408), [X](https://x.com/i/status/2122793141610672500), [Yonhap](https://en.yna.co.kr/view/AEN20261117010700315), [X](https://x.com/i/status/2122783455452778725), [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/18/oil-prices-fall-as-higher-us-crude-stocks-temper-supply-risks.html), [X](https://x.com/i/status/2122815860477747591)
articles.why: US LNG has replaced Russian pipeline gas as Europe’s main supplier. US officials present the price gap as a selling point for American energy, while for European industry it is a competitive handicap. Washington is pushing the same deal on Asian allies, linking investment pledges to trade terms. Energy dependence is no longer on Moscow but on Washington’s export and pricing policy.
articles.watch: P-TEC ministerial on 19 November (any LNG or nuclear deals, the Commission’s position); the EU gas-storage trajectory (IEA, 20:30 edition: lowest since 2013); Hormuz traffic; Korean decision on Alaska LNG.

articles.headline: European start-ups head for $81 billion this year, less than a fifth of the $450 billion going to US start-ups
articles.summary:
**Atomico’s annual State of European Tech report, published on 18 November, expects European technology start-ups to raise $81 billion in 2026.**

That is 62% more than last year and the second-highest total since the survey began in 2015, but far below the $450 billion expected for US start-ups. German start-ups are set to raise $13.4 billion (+89%), mostly going to established companies. Military AI developer Helsing, robot maker Neura Robotics and drone maker Quantum Systems have each raised more than $1 billion in recent months. “All the ingredients are actually there: talent, capital and demand. But they are either blocked or misallocated,” Atomico partner Tom Wehmeier told Reuters. Europeans hold $50 trillion in savings, but “only 0.01 per cent of that flows into European venture capital”.

**Sources:** [channelnewsasia.com](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/business/european-tech-startups-set-second-strongest-funding-year-6560591), [@ReutersTech](https://x.com/i/status/2122859922408841709)
articles.why: The gap explains why European start-ups end up selling to US buyers or moving to the US. Europe’s savings exist, but they are spread across 27 national markets with no single capital market to channel them into European technology. Europe has resources; what it lacks, time and again, is the scale that only joint action can provide.
articles.watch: The full Atomico report (country breakdown, defence-tech share); the Commission’s savings and investments union.

articles.headline: Update: Beijing’s commerce ministry threatens countermeasures if Washington keeps its global chip rule
articles.summary:
**At 13:20 Madrid (20:20 Beijing) China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) published its own answer to the US remote-access rule that the 13:30 edition led with.**

Until then only the Foreign Ministry had spoken. The spokesperson said the US “has generalized the concept of national security, abused export controls, and arbitrarily interfered in the normal trade and cooperation between Chinese enterprises and those of other countries”. The ministry added that the rule departs from the “important consensus reached by the two heads of state”, undermines “market rules and the international economic and trade order” and disrupts the stability of global semiconductor supply chains. It asked Washington to “return to the right track of resolving differences through consultation and cooperation”. Then came the warning: “Should the US side insist on going its own way, China will take countermeasures to firmly safeguard its national sovereignty, security and development interests.” Bloomberg reported it as China warning the US that it would retaliate. @F_CEAFE reposted Global Times’ account of the statement (Chinese state media), as well as its earlier coverage of the rule.

**Linked action–reaction:** the US Commerce rule of 16 November (BIS, written “by and at the direction of” Treasury and the NSC) → MFA, 17 November: “typical economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction” (13:30 edition) → MOFCOM, 17 November: a conditional threat of countermeasures. MOFCOM, not the MFA, is the body that runs China’s Unreliable Entity List and its export-control lists, including rare earths, so its words carry operational weight.
articles.why: the rule applies to data centres anywhere in the world, the EU included, and Europe is caught between both sides. If Beijing retaliates through rare earths or its own export controls, European industry will pay as a bystander for a measure that Brussels neither negotiated nor approved. TNW notes that the dispute comes days before Xi Jinping hosts Donald Trump at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, and that the tariff truce from last year ends in January, according to Bloomberg. The EU has no seat at that table, even though its data-centre operators and its supply chains are on it.
articles.watch: whether MOFCOM puts US firms on the Unreliable Entity List or tightens rare-earth licensing before the Shenzhen summit; whether the Commission says anything at all about a US rule that covers EU data centres.

articles.headline: Update: Nvidia sets up a board committee on export controls, and Jensen Huang will face three House committees on 1 December
articles.summary:
**On 17 November NVIDIA’s board created a standing **National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee** to oversee national-security policies, export-control compliance and global trade-risk management.**

Suzanne Nora Johnson chairs it, and Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri are members. The committee will meet at least quarterly and may hire independent legal, national-security and trade-compliance experts. The WSJ and Reuters described it as the company’s first big move since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO over his relationship with a woman US officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence. The same day, the House Select Committee on the CCP announced that Huang and NVIDIA general counsel Tim Teter had “voluntarily agreed” to appear before it, the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the House Intelligence Committee. These are closed-door, transcribed interviews, not public hearings: Huang on 1 December and Teter on 2 December. The chairmen (Moolenaar, Mast, Crawford) say Americans “need answers on Mr. Huang and NVIDIA’s role in allowing dangerous PRC actors to access our most advanced chips”. @F_CEAFE reposted both the NVIDIA release and the committee’s statement. On markets, Bloomberg reported that emerging-market stocks fell to a seven-month low as the tech selloff extended ahead of Nvidia’s earnings, and Reuters wrote that the “Nvidia turmoil marks the end of easy money for the AI trade”.
articles.why: the world’s key AI-chip supplier now has a board body that answers, in practice, to Washington’s national-security agenda, and Congress is turning chip sales into an intelligence matter. European cloud and AI projects depend on that supplier. Every tightening of its compliance will reach European customers too (see the remote-access rule, topic 1), and no European chip can replace it in this class.
articles.watch: Nvidia’s quarterly results this week; what the 1 December interview reveals about chip diversion through Southeast Asia (Megaspeed case, 13:30 edition).

articles.headline: Berlin rewrites its takeover law after UniCredit’s creeping approach on Commerzbank
articles.summary:
**According to a finance ministry draft seen by Reuters and Börsen-Zeitung, Germany will tighten its takeover rules to stop “low-ball” bids and “creeping in”.**

Today a bidder must make a mandatory offer when it reaches 30% of the voting rights. The draft adds further mandatory-offer thresholds at **35%, 40%, 45% and 50%**, so a bidder can no longer start with a minimum-price offer and then build its stake step by step. It also brings in a “put up or shut up” rule: if takeover speculation emerges, the target can demand an answer within four weeks, and a bidder that declines or stays silent cannot announce an offer for six months. Bidders would also have to disclose short derivatives and the instruments held by their counterparties, such as investment banks, even below the normal reporting thresholds. Börsen-Zeitung says UniCredit built part of its Commerzbank stake that way without the market knowing. The reform is meant to take effect in the first quarter of 2027 and, according to the ministry, will not apply to the UniCredit–Commerzbank deal, which Brussels cleared this week (2030 edition of 16 November). The federal government still holds 12.5% of Commerzbank.
articles.why: this is an intra-European deal (Italy’s UniCredit buying Germany’s Commerzbank), the kind of cross-border consolidation that Banking Union was supposed to allow. Germany’s answer is to raise national barriers. The tools themselves (more transparency, protecting minority shareholders) are reasonable and line up with EU law. But the trigger is telling: a large member state is building new defences against a European bidder, not a US or Chinese one. Europe keeps a fragmented banking market of national champions, while US banks operate at continental scale.
articles.watch: reactions from Rome and the Commission; whether other member states copy the “put up or shut up” rule.

articles.headline: Vestas asks Brussels to keep Chinese software out of Europe’s energy grids, and invokes reciprocity with Beijing
articles.summary:
**Henrik Andersen, CEO of the Danish wind-turbine maker Vestas, told Reuters that the EU should say a “very upfront ‘no thank you’” to Chinese components and technology with a software element in critical energy infrastructure.**

“The energy assets you build now last 30 to 50 years, and you have to make sure you can control them yourself,” he said. He proposed that about half of EU wind assets be made in Europe, and that control systems and software be treated separately from that requirement. Andersen recalled that China already applies this logic: Chinese authorities told Vestas it could no longer monitor the sensors of its own turbines in China or update their software remotely from Europe. “China put a marker in the sand five years ago, and now it’s time that we say that marker counts on both sides.” He rejected a blanket ban on Chinese parts, but asked for equal market access: “Eleven a side and a referee in the middle.” China’s Ming Yang replied that it stores all turbine data in Europe and allows no remote access without the operator’s approval. MOFCOM has threatened “strong countermeasures” if the EU adopts its revised Cybersecurity Act.
articles.why: this is a clear case of the reciprocity CEAFE calls for. China shut a European firm out of its own turbines, while Europe is still debating whether it may do the same. The key distinction is to protect control of critical infrastructure on Europe’s own terms, without importing US blacklists. As with chips (topic 1), whoever holds the software holds the switch. (Andersen’s company would also gain if Chinese rivals are kept out, as Reuters notes.)
articles.watch: the trilogue on the revised Cybersecurity Act; any MOFCOM response.

articles.headline: Spain’s Hernández de Cos moves closer to the ECB presidency in a Franco-German package
articles.summary:
**Germany’s finance ministry put forward Princeton economist Markus Brunnermeier as the European Central Bank’s next chief economist, replacing Philip Lane, whose term ends in May.**

The cabinet is due to approve the nomination on Wednesday 18 November, the deadline for submissions to the Eurogroup. According to Reuters (via RTÉ) and the Irish Times, the move seals a package agreed between Merz and Macron. Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos would succeed Christine Lagarde, who leaves early on 7 February, and France would take the markets-operations seat left by Isabel Schnabel in January. Laurence Boone is the likely French candidate, according to the Irish Times. The Dutch candidate Klaas Knot is expected to withdraw. An EU official quoted by the Irish Times called the three-way package a “done deal” now that Spain and Italy back de Cos. EU leaders are expected to endorse it at a summit next week, before the European Parliament is consulted.
articles.why: for the first time a Spaniard would lead the euro’s central bank, and a German would hold the chief economist’s post for the first time since 2011. The euro is the EU’s most federal instrument and its main tool of monetary sovereignty against the dollar. Even so, the board is shared out by national quota (France, Germany and Italy in practice hold permanent seats), and leaders are hurrying to finish before the 2027 French election and possible stress on French bonds.
articles.watch: German cabinet decision (18 November); the EU summit next week.

articles.headline: WTO: trade restrictions in force hit a record $5.4 trillion, as the US signs deal after deal on its own terms
articles.summary:
**The WTO Trade Monitoring Report, presented on 17 November and reposted by @F_CEAFE, finds that members introduced **333 new restrictive or non-facilitating measures in the first half of 2026**, more than the 300 recorded in all of 2025.**

They cover $2.0 trillion (8.0%) of world imports and $794 billion (3.2%) of exports. The stock of such measures introduced since 2009 and still in force reached a record: **$5.4 trillion, or 21.3% of world imports**, and $1.5 trillion (6.3%) of world exports, as of 30 June 2026. The WTO also notes that trade-facilitating measures increased. The same day in Manila, Donald Trump and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul signed a joint statement on the “substantial conclusion” of a US–Thailand Agreement on Reciprocal Trade. Trump says Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on US exports, remove non-tariff barriers on US vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol and poultry, and buy about $2.6 billion of extra US farm goods. The White House statement lists no US concessions. According to the Bangkok Post, the 2025 framework provides for a 19% baseline US tariff on Thai goods, and since July Thailand has also faced an extra 12.5% tariff from a forced-labour investigation. @F_CEAFE reposted the White House clip.
articles.why: the figures confirm the drift from multilateral rules to bilateral deals in which Washington sets the terms one partner at a time: tariffs scrapped on one side, a baseline tariff kept on the other, plus purchase commitments. The EU, the largest trading bloc and the one most attached to the WTO, is losing the system that protected it. It negotiates with Washington under the same asymmetry, despite being much larger than Thailand.
articles.watch: signature of the US–Thailand agreement “in the coming weeks”; other ASEAN deals around the Manila summit.

articles.headline: Update: Washington extends its chip controls to data centres worldwide, and Beijing calls it “economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction”
articles.summary:
**On 16 November the US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule on remote access to advanced “super intelligence” (SI) chips and servers.**

BIS says the rule was “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council” and that it is meant to stop existing restrictions from being circumvented “through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries”. The rule adds a new end-use control: a licence is required to ship advanced chips and servers to a data centre **anywhere in the world** that provides more than 12 million “aggregate TPP” of compute to companies headquartered (or whose ultimate parent is headquartered) in China, another Country Group D:5 destination or Macau. That means European data centres are covered too, if they serve such customers. Data centres already serving those customers must obtain a licence within 90 days or “face future export restrictions”, and exports of advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil now need a licence because of a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to China. The same day, White House science and technology director Michael Kratsios announced the carrot that goes with the stick: Commerce designated 33 preset consortia under the “American SI Exports Program”, full-stack US AI packages backed by priority licensing, advocacy and financing from Commerce, State, EXIM, DFC, USTDA, Treasury, USTR and SBA, so that “U.S. technology [is] the easiest, most attractive choice for allies and partners”. @F_CEAFE reposted the House China Select Committee’s announcement, Kratsios’s post, the Commerce–Justice statement on the Megaspeed probe, an analyst’s thread on the rule and, at 11:09 Madrid, the Chinese Foreign Ministry’s response.

**China’s reaction (linked):** At the MFA’s regular press conference on 17 November, spokesperson Guo Jiakun said: “The move is yet another case of the U.S. overstretching the concept of national security, and abusing export control measures to interfere in normal trade and tech cooperation between China and other countries and go after China’s high-tech industry. Such typical economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction run counter to the common understandings between the two countries, harm the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies, and disrupt global supply chains. China will do what is necessary to firmly safeguard its legitimate and lawful rights and interests.” Asked about Megaspeed, he said China’s position on US chip exports to China “is consistent”. On MOFCOM’s Spokesman’s Remarks page, the latest item at about 11:45 Madrid was still the 13 November statement on the Unreliable Entity List, so the ministry had not issued a separate statement yet. Global Times (Chinese state media) and CGTN (Chinese state media) carried the MFA line, and CGTN framed it as China accusing the US of “economic coercion and overreach”.
articles.why: This is an extraterritorial rule in the full sense. A US agency, acting on Treasury and NSC instructions, now decides which customers a data centre in Frankfurt, Dublin or Madrid may serve if it runs American chips. The rule removes the de minimis exemption for this end use and expects data centres to hand their “know your customer” checks to exporters, where a refusal counts as a red flag. Europe has no chip of its own in this class: the continent’s fastest supercomputer, JUPITER, runs on NVIDIA GH200. EU cloud and AI providers therefore follow Washington’s China policy whether or not the EU has agreed to it, just as Europeans already did on Iranian and Venezuelan oil, Huawei in 5G networks and the frozen EU–China investment agreement (CAI). The “American SI Exports Program” finishes the picture: allies are offered subsidised US stacks on condition of “trusted” use. Beijing’s warning of “necessary measures” could land on European firms caught in the middle, as the Nexperia case showed. Here is another example of why Europeans need to act together: only a common European compute and chip base would let Europe decide its own export rules.
articles.watch: Federal Register publication (19 Nov) and the start of the 90-day clock; whether MOFCOM announces countermeasures (Unreliable Entity List, rare-earth or other export controls); whether the Commission or the Dutch, Irish and German governments say anything on the rule’s reach into EU data centres; the Trump–Xi meeting in Shenzhen (19 Nov) and the US–China truce that runs to 10 January. Earlier coverage: 16 Nov 07:30–20:30 and 17 Nov 07:30.

articles.headline: Megaspeed: Washington details a chip-smuggling dragnet that runs through Singapore
articles.summary:
**The US Commerce and Justice departments released a joint statement on their investigation of Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud-computing company and Nvidia customer.**

According to the statement as reported by CNBC and SCMP, Commerce began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 for possible export-control violations and asked Nvidia for its sales records in May 2025; Nvidia put Megaspeed on its “no sell” list in June 2025, and the Justice Department then took over the criminal investigation. The statement also says 17 defendants in six separate investigations have been charged with smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of semiconductors. Vice President JD Vance said the administration was concerned about any reports that a third country had obtained Nvidia technology (Reuters post). Singapore is now seeking talks with Washington on the AI chip rules (SCMP). Separately, Reuters reported in an exclusive that Chinese entities are using increasingly sophisticated ways to use output from leading American AI models to train domestic rivals as chip curbs bite.
articles.why: The probe is the enforcement arm of the rule in topic 1. Third-country hubs like Singapore now carry the burden of proving their customers are clean, which is exactly what European data centres will be asked to do. A European AI industry that depends on US chips also inherits US investigations, “no sell” lists and the legal risk Nvidia is now passing on to its buyers (CNBC via Reuters post).
articles.watch: charges or Entity List designations tied to Megaspeed; Singapore–US talks; Nvidia’s results and its new export-control board committee.

articles.headline: China’s envoy in Madrid: Europe should “not follow the instructions of others” on ASML chip-tool exports
articles.summary:
**In an interview with Reuters in Madrid, Qu Xun, China’s minister-counsellor in Spain, said long-standing Dutch limits on exporting ASML chipmaking equipment to China are casting a shadow over EU–China industrial-policy talks.**

“We want the European Union to make its own decisions and not follow the instructions of others,” he said, adding: “We want to import ASML goods.” He warned that “Europe is forbidding it because it is afraid China will rob its technology… If Europe thinks that way, China will too”, implying that China could limit the sharing of its own technology. Reuters notes that the Netherlands has restricted ASML exports to China since 2019 and that the US is pushing for curbs on lower-level machines, with stricter controls under discussion in Congress that would also hit Japan’s Tokyo Electron. Qu said China seeks “equality and reciprocity” as the EU weighs local-content, technology-transfer and ownership conditions on foreign investors in EVs, batteries and cars. He also said Chinese investment in Spain has tripled in a decade to €12 billion, with SAIC, Chery, CATL and AESC among the investors.
articles.why: This is the other side of topic 1. ASML is Europe’s one undisputed world chokepoint in semiconductors, and its exports to China are set by Dutch licences shaped by US pressure. Beijing is now openly linking that alignment to Europe’s access to Chinese battery and EV technology, which is exactly what Spain is trying to attract. CEAFE’s point is that Europe should decide its export policy as a bloc, on its own interests, rather than member by member under pressure from either Washington or Beijing.
articles.watch: any Dutch or Commission reply; US congressional moves on chip-tool controls; MOFCOM’s line on EU investment conditions.

articles.headline: TOP500: China keeps the world’s fastest supercomputer on a fully Chinese stack, while Europe’s best runs on American chips
articles.why: Measured together, the EU-27 is a real second pole in supercomputing; measured country by country, no member state comes close to the US or China. Europe’s flagship machine depends on US processors, the very kind of hardware whose use Washington now regulates worldwide, whereas China has built its No. 1 on its own chips, interconnect and operating system. The European Processor Initiative and EuroHPC exist precisely to close that gap. The EU as a whole can bear comparison; each capital on its own cannot. That is the difference that matters.
articles.watch: next list June 2027; EuroHPC’s next exascale system (Alice Recoque, France). Rankings file updated.

articles.headline: China’s Sinochem cuts its Pirelli stake to 13.6% after Italy’s “golden power” curbs
articles.summary:
**Marco Polo International Italy, the vehicle of Chinese state-owned Sinochem (CNRC), sold 70 million Pirelli shares (6.5% of the capital) in an accelerated bookbuild run by BNP Paribas at €6.50 per share, about €455 million, a 3.8% discount to Monday’s close.**

Its stake falls from 20.1% to about 13.6%, behind Marco Tronchetti Provera’s Camfin/MTP (29.9%) and Czech billionaire Michal Strnad (about 14%), who bought 14% from Sinochem earlier this year at the same price. Pirelli shares fell more than 3% in Milan. The retreat follows Rome’s use of its “golden power” screening: an April decree limited Sinochem to three of the 15 board seats, with no executive roles or strategic powers, and those restrictions apply while its stake exceeds 9.99%. Italian press links the intervention to protecting Pirelli’s Cyber Tyre technology and the company’s access to the US tyre market. A 90-day lock-up applies to the remaining stake (Websim/Intermonte).
articles.why: This is the European version of the “blocking Chinese control” track the owner asked us to follow: a member state used FDI screening to push a Chinese state shareholder out of a strategic industrial company, partly so as not to lose access to the US market. Italian screening worked, but it was a national decision; the EU still has no common instrument to decide such cases, and alignment with US connected-vehicle rules is shaping European ownership choices. Note: @F_CEAFE has not posted this story.
articles.watch: whether Sinochem drops below 10% after the lock-up, lifting the golden-power conditions; any MOFCOM or Sinochem comment.

articles.headline: Commission autumn forecast: growth holds at 1.2% in the euro area, but the energy shock keeps inflation above 3%
articles.summary:
**The European Commission’s Autumn 2026 Economic Forecast (17 November) expects EU GDP growth of 1.4% in 2026 and 2027 and 1.5% in 2028, and 1.2%, 1.2% and 1.3% in the euro area.**

Inflation is forecast at 3.3% (EU) and 3.2% (euro area) in 2026, easing to 2.3% and 2.1% only in 2028. The Commission blames the Middle East war: energy flows through Hormuz “remain severely disrupted”, Brent exceeded $100 in October, diesel prices doubled year on year and TTF gas traded above €95/MWh in late October, more than three times its late-February level, with thin buffers in strategic reserves and gas storage. Central banks, including the Fed, have started or are expected to raise rates, and the 10-year US Treasury yield was about 5.1% at the cut-off. Deficits widen to −3.6% of GDP in the EU in 2026 and −3.8% in 2028. Bloomberg summarised it as robust growth despite stubborn inflation.
articles.why: The forecast puts a number on Europe’s energy dependence: imported fossil fuels are again the main driver of inflation and of the rate rises that tighten financing for defence and industrial investment. The Commission itself lists faster progress in the energy transition “to reduce Europe’s dependence on imported fossil fuels” and stronger investment in defence and industry as upside factors.
articles.watch: Eurostat’s final October HICP; the ECB’s December meeting.

articles.headline: Brussels sets a precedent: EU anti-dumping duties now count the knock-on effect of Chinese overcapacity
articles.summary:
**The European Commission imposed definitive anti-dumping duties on 16 November on cold-rolled flat steel from India, Japan, Taiwan, Türkiye and Vietnam.**

For the first time in an EU trade-defence case it established “Particular Market Situations”, which let it construct the normal value instead of using distorted domestic prices. In India the distortion came from government measures on the price of iron ore. In Taiwan, the Commission found that Chinese overcapacity had pushed Chinese cold-rolled steel into the Taiwanese market, depressing local prices and the profitability of Taiwanese producers. In other words, Brussels now treats the price-depressing effect of Chinese overcapacity on third countries as something it can correct for (the “push-out” effect, in the words of the law firm Gide, which worked on the case). The Commission calls the investigation “of systemic importance for trade defence, beyond the products and industry sectors it concerns”, and Bloomberg reports that it is preparing further tools and assessing safeguards for chemicals and machinery.

**China’s reaction (linked):** No MOFCOM statement on this case was found by 05:45 Madrid. MOFCOM has already criticised France and Germany’s request for stronger EU trade-defence tools (10 October) and reports of a European “Section 301”-style instrument (30 September). Watch MOFCOM’s next briefing.
articles.why: This is the EU using its own legal toolbox to protect a strategic industry (12 producing member states, more than 8,600 jobs), rather than copying Washington’s tariffs. The duties hit partners, not China directly, so the real test is whether Brussels uses the same reasoning against the source of the overcapacity, and against anyone else, including the US, whose subsidies distort markets. A Union of 27 can set precedents like this. No member state alone could.
articles.watch: MOFCOM reaction; whether the new trade-defence tools and the chemicals and machinery safeguards are announced; whether partners such as India or Japan challenge the duties at the WTO.

articles.headline: Update: The chip rule hits Asian markets as Trump’s aides fight over China
articles.summary:
**New facts since the 20:30 edition: Monday’s sell-off in Taiwan was the second-largest one-day point loss in the TAIEX’s history, at −6.03% to 41,040.**

TSMC fell 5.74%, Foxconn 9.34% and MediaTek 7.89%, with 17 high-priced stocks limit-down (Taiwan News). Barclays blamed forced retail liquidation. On Tuesday morning, after the BIS rule, the Nikkei was down 0.9% (Advantest −3.9%, SoftBank −3.8%), the Kospi was down 1.0% (Samsung −2.0%, SK hynix −1.1%) and Singapore was down 0.6% (Dow Jones/MarketScreener). UOB estimates that the move erased about $960 bn in US tech market value. Bloomberg reports that Chinese model developer Z.ai has fallen 85% from its peak as chip fears hit Chinese AI firms. In Washington, the Washington Post and WSJ describe an open feud between Treasury Secretary Bessent and Commerce Secretary Lutnick over Nvidia chips. Hours after the crackdown, Trump said he understood “both sides”.

**China’s reaction (linked):** Still no MOFCOM statement on the final rule by 05:45 Madrid. The latest official line found is the Foreign Ministry’s of 13 November: China “opposes abuse of export control measures” and urges both sides to deliver on the “common understandings between the two presidents”. Watch the Shenzhen summit.
articles.why: Washington’s chip policy now moves markets across Asia and is being made through a personal fight inside the cabinet. That is a fragile base for European clouds and for ASML, which must comply with it. Europe still has no equivalent lever of its own.
articles.watch: Trump–Xi summit in Shenzhen; MOFCOM; European chip stocks (ASML, Infineon, STMicro) at today’s open.

articles.headline: Macron in Kuala Lumpur: rare earths and defence, as Malaysia questions Western suppliers
articles.summary:
**President Emmanuel Macron is meeting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim on 17 November, on his first visit to Malaysia since 2017, to upgrade relations to a “strategic partnership” and sign several MoUs on defence, trade, the energy transition and critical minerals.**

Macron said that a key aim is to diversify France’s sources of rare earths: “having several sources of supply means reducing the risk of having to halt production lines”. The French firm Carester and the Malaysian miner Malaco are working on a mining and processing project that includes a separation plant in Perak with an estimated capacity of about 13,000 tonnes of rare earths a year. France is also offering help on Malaysia’s move from chip packaging into chip design. Malaysia is reassessing foreign arms suppliers after Norway revoked an export licence for missiles for its navy. Its defence minister said this raised questions about the trustworthiness of Western and NATO partners (France 24/Reuters).
articles.why: It is a concrete European move to break China’s grip on rare earths without relying on US-led clubs. But it is still one member state acting alone, and it competes with Germany’s and others’ efforts. The Norway episode shows how export-licence politics can close markets to European industry. Pooled EU purchasing and stockpiling of critical raw materials, and predictable European export rules, would carry more weight than national deals.
articles.watch: Texts of the MoUs signed today; any defence contract; EU Critical Raw Materials Act projects.

articles.headline: Update: Oil drops below $93 despite more tanker attacks; Houthis close in on Bab el-Mandeb
articles.summary:
**New facts since the 20:30 edition: Brent settled down 3.6% at $92.44 a barrel on Monday and WTI 3.2% lower at $85.72.**

In Asian trading on Tuesday Brent was around $92. Recovering Middle East exports point to a surplus: the IEA expects the market to return to surplus in Q4, and Saudi Arabia pumped 10.5 mb/d in October (ANZ). The risks have not gone away, though. The IRGC claims that two more tankers hit mines (not independently verified), UKMTO reported two tanker attacks off Khasab, Oman, and the IMO has recorded 136 security incidents involving vessels in the region since 1 March, 35 of them in October. In Yemen, Houthi fighters have advanced to about 100 km from Aden after government forces left positions near the Bab el-Mandeb, the strait used by Saudi crude shipped from Yanbu, which has been the kingdom’s main export outlet since the Iran war began. Iran warns of severe gas shortages this winter (Al Jazeera, Reuters).
articles.why: Cheaper oil hides a fragile supply: both chokepoints feeding Europe and Asia are contested at once. Europe has no naval or energy-security instrument of its own at that scale, and it depends on Saudi rerouting and on US decisions. The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at its lowest since 1982 after a 172 m-barrel release, so Washington’s buffer is thinner too.
articles.watch: TTF and EU storage today; OPEC+ on 29 November; Houthi moves around Aden.

articles.headline: A US Pentagon loan props up Wolfspeed, Infineon’s silicon carbide wafer supplier
articles.summary:
**Wolfspeed (Durham, North Carolina), the silicon carbide (SiC) materials and power-chip maker, reported revenue of $155 m for the quarter to 27 September.**

That is down 21% year on year but up 3.6% on the previous quarter. Its net loss was $111.4 m. AI data centres were its fastest-growing market. The company is building its recovery on a conditional 30-year, $1.5 bn loan commitment from the US Department of War “to advance the domestic supply chain for wide-bandgap semiconductors”. The first $600 m tranche refinances costly debt, and later tranches would fund domestic GaN power devices, GaN-on-SiC RF materials and radiation-hardening capabilities. During the quarter Wolfspeed extended its long-term SiC wafer supply agreement with Germany’s Infineon from 150 mm to 200 mm wafers (Semiconductor Today).
articles.why: Washington treats SiC and GaN, which are key to electric vehicles, radar and electronic warfare, as national security and funds its champion through the defence budget. Europe’s largest power-semiconductor maker, Infineon, deepens its reliance on that US-backed supplier. Europe has SiC capacity of its own (STMicro in Catania, Soitec), and the EU Chips Act and EDF should treat this as a sovereignty issue in the same way.
articles.watch: Final terms of the US government loan; Infineon’s SiC sourcing strategy.

items.title: Economy — 2026-11-16 20:30
headlines: Update: Washington closes the “remote access” loophole and extends chip controls to data centres worldwide
Brussels clears UniCredit–Commerzbank, the largest cross-border bank deal since the financial crisis
Energy: oil slides to about $95 despite Hormuz mine attacks, but Europe’s gas cushion stays thin
China’s export-control lever: rare-earth champions double profits, tunnel-boring machine curbs start Wednesday
Reverse flow: Italy’s Maire buys US LNG liquefaction technology from Baker Hughes
A €1 bn fund for European deep tech: Plural, an early Helsing backer, closes Fund 3

articles.headline: Update: Washington closes the “remote access” loophole and extends chip controls to data centres worldwide
articles.summary:
**The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule on 16 November, “written by and at the direction of” the Treasury and the National Security Council, to stop companies headquartered in China and other Country Group D:5 destinations (or Macau) from using advanced US AI chips remotely through data centres in third countries.**

Any data centre anywhere in the world that supplies more than 12 million “aggregate TPP” of compute to such companies now needs a licence, and chip exporters, foundries and data-centre operators must check their customers’ direct and indirect ownership. The rule also adds a licence requirement for advanced chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, except when the buyer is a US-headquartered company, and formally rescinds the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. It comes three days before the Trump–Xi meeting in Shenzhen and after the Nvidia espionage scandal; a US senator has accused Commerce of failing to stem chip flows to China, while President Trump expressed confidence in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick (Reuters, Bloomberg). Previous coverage: 07:30 and 13:30 editions, topic 1.

**China’s reaction (linked):** No MOFCOM statement on the new rule was found by 18:45 Madrid. On 13 November, when the measure was still a bill, China’s Foreign Ministry opposed the “abuse” of export controls. Reuters quotes analysts saying that the scandal “is going to embolden China hawks and rock this very fragile trade truce”. Beijing’s counter-levers are covered in topic 5. Watch MOFCOM and the summit.

**ALERT — not yet reposted by @F_CEAFE:** US export-control story with extraterritorial reach to European data centres. No @F_CEAFE post on it in the window. Link: https://media.bis.gov/press-release/bis-issues-rule-addressing-remote-access-american-super-intelligence-technology
articles.why: The rule is extraterritorial. It applies to data centres “to or within any destination worldwide”, including European clouds, which must now vet their customers’ ownership for Washington. It also writes a US-only exemption into law: in the five “diversion-risk” countries, chips for US-headquartered companies need no licence, but chips for European ones do. This is the US double standard in regulatory form, with American industrial leadership treated as national security and enforced on allies’ soil. Europe has no comparable instrument to protect its own technology and complies through ASML and its cloud operators without reciprocity.
articles.watch: Federal Register publication and comment period; MOFCOM response; Trump–Xi Shenzhen summit (19 Nov); whether the Commission or EU cloud providers comment on the due-diligence burden.

articles.headline: Brussels clears UniCredit–Commerzbank, the largest cross-border bank deal since the financial crisis
articles.summary:
**The European Commission gave unconditional approval on 16 November under the EU Merger Regulation to UniCredit’s acquisition of control of Commerzbank, Germany’s second-largest bank.**

The US Federal Reserve also approved it the same day, and UniCredit expects the last outstanding approval by the end of November. Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera called it “probably the biggest cross-border banking deal we have had since the financial crisis” and a model of “positive scaling up of EU banks”. Unusually, she warned that Brussels would “react accordingly” if a national government tried to block completion (Politico). Berlin, which still holds about 13% of Commerzbank, is demanding guarantees on jobs, the Frankfurt headquarters and two supervisory-board seats.
articles.why: This is a European champion built inside the single market, not a sale to an outside buyer. Even combined, UniCredit and Commerzbank would be worth only about a fifth of JPMorgan (Politico). That gap is the scale argument for the banking union and for capital-markets integration that can finance European defence and industry. It also tests whether member states will put national control ahead of building European scale.
articles.watch: Berlin’s response; the final approval by end-November; the merger-guidelines reform.

articles.headline: Energy: oil slides to about $95 despite Hormuz mine attacks, but Europe’s gas cushion stays thin
articles.summary:
**Brent fell 0.7% to $95.15 a barrel and WTI to $88.19 on Monday (Reuters via CNBC), extending a two-week slide.**

The IEA said on Friday that the oil market will return to surplus in Q4, with supply at 105 mb/d, 1.7 mb/d above demand, as Middle East exports recover. This happened even though Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said two more tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, after six caught fire on Sunday and Monday (claims not independently verified). Dutch TTF gas slipped below €90/MWh on milder weather, the expected end of Norway’s Troll outage and record pipeline flows to US LNG plants (21.8 bcf on Saturday, BloombergNEF). EU storage, however, was 70.5% full on 14 November, 19.5 points below the five-year norm, and QatarEnergy has extended its force majeure until at least the end of December. Previous coverage: 13:30 edition, topic 3.
articles.why: Lower prices come from US LNG and an IEA stock release, not from European resilience. Europe is swapping dependence on Gulf and Russian gas for dependence on US cargoes, which are exactly what Washington asks it to buy. The low storage level leaves the winter exposed to any new shock.
articles.watch: EU storage trajectory against the 1 December target; Qatar force majeure; Hormuz shipping data.

articles.headline: China’s export-control lever: rare-earth champions double profits, tunnel-boring machine curbs start Wednesday
articles.summary:
**China’s two rare-earth national champions more than doubled their nine-month profits.**

China Northern Rare Earth earned 3.65 bn yuan ($547 m) and China Rare Earth Resources and Technology 408 m yuan, as production quotas and consolidation pushed prices up (Reuters via Mining Weekly). NdPr oxide, the main magnet input, trades at 719,000 yuan a tonne, 62% above its level when the April 2025 export controls were introduced. Common magnets are not controlled, and China exported 48,057 t of them in January–September, up from 39,826 t a year earlier. Separately, Beijing’s new export controls on tunnel-boring machines take effect on 18 November. Exports to “sensitive” countries with territorial disputes, including India, will need a MOFCOM licence, which could delay metro, high-speed-rail and Himalayan-border tunnelling projects (The Hindu, Times of India). Bloomberg notes that US dependence on Chinese supplies “goes far beyond” rare earths.
articles.why: This is the counterpart to topic 1. China answers US controls with its own, and the profits show that the lever pays. Europe faces the same dependence on Chinese rare earths but neither builds an equivalent lever nor answers either side. The Critical Raw Materials Act targets are the test.
articles.watch: Whether Beijing uses rare earths against the BIS rule after the summit; how India responds to the tunnel-boring machine licences.

articles.headline: Reverse flow: Italy’s Maire buys US LNG liquefaction technology from Baker Hughes
articles.summary:
**Maire’s Nextchem unit agreed to buy Chart Industries’ mid-scale IPSMR and small-scale LNG process technologies, with more than 90 patents, for $220 million in cash.**

Chart is a wholly owned subsidiary of Baker Hughes. The deal includes a 10-year cold-box supply agreement and a 12-person team, and is expected to close by the end of 2026 or in early January 2027, subject to regulatory approvals (Maire press release, 15 Nov). Maire shares rose 3.6% on Monday (Reuters).
articles.why: This time a European firm acquires US intellectual property and know-how in a strategic energy technology, the opposite of the usual flow of European technology into US hands. It gives Europe a licensing position in LNG liquefaction at a time when European energy security depends on LNG. Watch whether US authorities impose conditions.
articles.watch: Regulatory approvals before closing.

articles.headline: A €1 bn fund for European deep tech: Plural, an early Helsing backer, closes Fund 3
articles.summary:
**UK-based Plural raised €1 billion ($1.1 bn) for its third fund to back European start-ups in energy, AI infrastructure, defence and healthcare.**

Two-thirds will go to early-stage deals and one-third to follow-ons (Reuters via StreetInsider, TechCrunch). In a post reposted on the R&D list on 16 November, Commissioner Ekaterina Zaharieva highlighted the €5 billion Scaleup Europe Fund at the European Startup and Scaleup Forum.
articles.why: Private European capital going into defence and AI start-ups reduces the need to sell growing companies to US buyers. Fund sizes still lag US venture capital, and the Scaleup Europe Fund is meant to close that late-stage gap.
articles.watch: First investments; Scaleup Europe Fund deployment.
